articles.title: Nvidia director sold nearly $1B in stock weeks before the Jensen Huang scandal
articles.body:
Nvidia director sold nearly $1B in stock weeks before the Jensen Huang scandal broke — and no trading plan was flagged
Nvidia's second-largest shareholder sold about $946 million in company stock in the months leading up to CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Nov. 12.
Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] Board Director Mark Stevens was one of the top AI sellers in Q3 2026, selling roughly 4.2 million shares, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. There were three separate batches of stock sales from Stevens, who joined the Nvidia board in 2008 following an earlier stint as a director from 1993 to 2006.
Must Read
- Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
The first common stock sale took place from Aug. 31 to Sept. 2 at equity prices ranging from $220 to $226, generating $411 million in new cash. The second sale stretched from Sept. 3 to Sept. 4 at prices ranging between $227 to $234 per share, garnering about $236 million. The third sale occurred on Sept. 18 at roughly $220 per share, netting roughly $300 million.
Still holding plenty of Nvidia stock
Prearranged trading plans are used by executives to buy or sell shares of their firm on specific dates or target prices. It's a mechanism to wall off company employees from insider trading accusations as long as they stick to the automatic plan.
The SEC first instituted the practice in 2000 and modified it in 2022 to include a 90-day waiting period for starting trades. In some cases, the plans were abused by executives in instances like executing share sales just before an earnings report.
In Stevens's case, he didn't have such a trading plan, but that's not necessarily a red flag on its own. Insiders cashing out of their stock will do so for a variety of reasons that aren't always tied to a company's performance, such as quickly raising liquidity. In Nvidia's case, the move could pour water on the enthusiasm of retail investors to buy into an AI titan that has also attracted short sellers.
The first two stock sales in late August and early September followed a robust Q2 earnings report that caused Nvidia shares to jump about 10% in valuein the following week. Stevens still holds about 27.5 million shares in Nvidia, a colossal position.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.body:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

If you've ever used a high-quality bread knife to slice a crusty sourdough loaf, you know the difference it makes. Made In's fully-forged bread knife is an excellent choice, as it stays sharp for years, delivering optimal performance with every loaf. This versatile,editor-loved Dutch oven is a piece you'll use for a lifetime. Though it's a hefty 14 pounds, that weight is a benefit, ensuring exceptional heat retention. It's also a great way to add a vibrant pop of color to your stovetop, available in Harbour Blue, Antique White, and three seasonal colors.
Stylish and functional, this Made In set is a must-have for any tea enthusiast. The stainless steel kettle features a built-in temperature gauge, precise spout, and ergonomic handle with a built-in sleeve; plus, its sleek design will look great on your stovetop. It comes with four stackable mugs that are stain- and chip-resistant, with a comfortable handle and wide opening. Choose from plain white or the red- or blue-trim option.
A nonstick frying pan is an absolute must-have for almost every home cook. Not only can you prepare nearly any dish in it, but it can also significantly simplify the cleanup. Made In offers a versatile version, perfect for everything from sautéing vegetables and whipping up a stir-fry to flipping pancakes and crafting the ideal omelet. articles.title: Live-migration support in FreeBSD and bhyve coming
articles.body:
This project presents a first working state for live migration of bhyve guests on FreeBSD 15.1. A running amd64 guest can move between two hosts over TCP while continuing to run; it is paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. The work builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support and adds dirty-page tracking in the vmm kernel module together with a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.
I previously discussed the state of bhyve live migration, its historical development, existing limitations, and why it matters for the future of FreeBSD virtualization in my article bhyve on FreeBSD and VM Live Migration – Quo vadis?.
The goal is deliberately practical: make it possible to test, discuss, and improve a real implementation rather than discuss live migration only in the abstract. The current code and test tooling are being published as a WIP RFC so that the next steps can be shaped in the open. A more detailed demonstration of a VM being live migrated can be watched on my YouTube channel.
Why this matters
Live migration is an important building block for enterprise virtualisation. It enables host maintenance, hardware replacement, load balancing, and failure-domain management with far less disruption to workloads. It is also central to the Sylve project, which aims to offer a Proxmox-like virtualisation solution for FreeBSD. Migration is not an optional convenience in that kind of platform; it is one of the capabilities that makes clustered operations practical.
It is equally important for BoxyBSD, where I offer free BSD-based VPS instances to individuals. Without a credible migration path, routine host work can require a guest outage. That makes live migration a current show stopper for the project, and is why this work is being pushed toward a testable, reviewable state.
How the current implementation works
The source starts with a pre-copy phase. It sends populated guest memory, then repeatedly obtains a bitmap of pages changed since the previous scan and sends only those pages. Once the remaining dirty set fits the configured downtime target, stops shrinking, or reaches the configured round limit, bhyve pauses the guest and its devices. It then sends the final dirty pages and the existing snapshot state for the vCPUs, kernel state, and emulated devices.
The destination validates the basic VM geometry, receives memory and state, restores it, and reports that it is ready. Only then does the source send GO, the commit point. Before GO, a failed migration can resume the source guest. The destination does not start the guest if it does not receive that commit message. A warm, stop-and-copy mode is available too, which is useful both as a fallback and as a comparison baseline.
What is implemented today
- Pre-copy and warm migration: live pre-copy is configurable with downtime and maximum-round controls; explicit stop-and-copy migration is also supported.
- Multi-vCPU protocol support: the migration handshake carries the guest vCPU count, the destination refuses a count mismatch, and all guest vCPUs are paused and resumed as part of migration. The published test bed has primarily exercised a one-vCPU guest, so multi-vCPU stress and race testing remain required before making broader claims.
- Memory consistency checks: dirty-page tracking covers guest and mapped emulation writes through page dirty state, while vmm write holds are recorded separately. The test workload rewrites and verifies guest memory and reports any missing or stale page as a mismatch. Repeated ping-pong migrations have been used to check that the workload continues without errors.
- Disk-write validation: a guest-side workload repeatedly writes and fsyncs files, verifies checksums, and is checked again after a cold reboot. This is intended to exercise the device pause, drain, and restore path.
- Failure handling: destination refusal, an unreachable target, and a target disappearing during both pre-copy and stop-and-copy have been tested. Before commit, the source is intended to resume the paused guest after failure.
- Basic destination checks: protocol version, page size, memory layout, and vCPU count are checked before data transfer. The migration socket is opened by bhyvectl and passed into bhyve so that bhyve can remain inside its Capsicum sandbox.
- Supported scope: this is amd64-only and depends on the experimental BHYVE_SNAPSHOT support. It relies on snapshot-capable emulated devices; PCI passthrough is not migratablem, yet.
Observed results
In the current two-host test environment, repeated live migrations, memory-rewrite workloads, and fsync-heavy disk workloads have completed successfully. For a slowly dirtying 512 MiB guest, observed downtime has been roughly 138–171 ms. A rapidly dirtying guest may not converge during pre-copy, but still falls back to a correct stop-and-copy completion with a longer pause. These are encouraging engineering results, not a production support promise or a complete correctness proof.
Blockers before upstreaming can be evaluated further
The following are neutral engineering requirements, not criticism of the value of the prototype. They need to be addressed first before further upstreaming into FreeBSD can be evaluated responsibly.
- Prove and harden dirty-log correctness. The kernel-side dirty-page algorithm must be demonstrated not to lose a write while dirty bits are examined and cleared. It needs focused concurrency, paging, emulation-write, and multi-vCPU stress coverage, plus a reviewable locking and memory-ordering argument.
- Define a complete compatibility contract. Matching memory size and vCPU count is not enough. A destination should verify guest identity, CPU capabilities, bhyve/vmm and snapshot format compatibility, device topology and capabilities, and shared-storage identity before accepting a migration.
- Harden the transport and protocol. The current TCP transport has no authentication or encryption and uses a first-version native protocol. A stable protocol needs explicit wire formats, bounded message handling, timeouts, version negotiation, authentication or a supported external secure transport model, and clear operational guidance.
- Clarify the commit and device-side-effect boundary. The source/destination handoff must be reviewed so that device restoration cannot cause externally visible work before the source has committed, and so that the unavoidable uncertain outcome after a lost post-commit acknowledgement is operationally recoverable.
- Specify storage and network handoff. Shared storage must have defined coherency, durability, and fencing assumptions. Network migration also needs a clear answer for tap/bridge handling, MAC/IP movement, and traffic convergence.
- Build an in-tree test strategy. The current scripts and test-bed workloads are useful, but upstream review will need automated regression coverage and a documented support matrix across CPU counts, memory sizes, supported devices, host CPUs, and failure cases.
- Separate the work into reviewable patches. Dirty-page tracking, snapshot API refactoring, protocol/receiver work, CLI changes, and tests should be independently reviewable. This will make design feedback more actionable and reduce the risk of merging coupled changes.
Next steps
We have already had deeper discussions about these questions in the Sylve Discord. Publishing this current state is intended to make those discussions more concrete, bring in wider FreeBSD and bhyve feedback, and turn the prototype into a clear roadmap. The immediate focus is correctness, compatibility validation, transport safety, and repeatable tests—not adding performance features first. Currently, some peopel already have access to it and it's planned ot publish this at least as a proposal on my git and GitHub at:
- git.gyptazy.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
- github.com/gyptazy/freebsd-bhyve-live-migration
Compression, zero-page elision, broader device coverage, richer orchestration, and performance tuning can follow once the foundation is sound. If you operate bhyve, work on FreeBSD virtualisation, or are interested in Sylve or BoxyBSD, testing the RFC and contributing design feedback would be especially valuable.
Status: WIP RFC for a first working bhyve live-migration implementation on FreeBSD 15.1.

articles.title: 6-11X speedup running Qwen3.6 on my RTX 4090, full repo.
articles.body:
Lightreason is a local inference lab and interactive Studio for running Qwen faster on one RTX 4090. The experiments use the original BF16 weights for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (3.09B parameters) and the text model of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (34.66B parameters).
- 3B · 63.0 → 139.6 tok/s across six prompts. LR CUDA graphs and compact KV matched all 30 Hugging Face timing runs. It also matched complete Python, JavaScript, and SQL responses in 9/9 new pairs. The separate PARD2 runner reached 58.3 → 525.2 tok/s on a complete matching weather response and 63.6 → 724.4 tok/s on the best matching 128-token Fibonacci slice. Performance · Coding benchmarks
- 35B · 7.93 → 51.08 tok/s on the capped Python prompt. The 6.44× comparison uses the same input across sessions. Output first differs from Scheduled at token 116. The packed configuration matched all 20 pairs against its closer fixed eight-position control. Performance · Coding results and output checks
The smaller model fits on the GPU, where reusing prepared GPU work and checking several tokens together saves time. The larger model’s text weights occupy 64.56 GiB. The 35B runner keeps most expert weights in system RAM and moves the ones Qwen actually uses. When a draft predicts several tokens, Qwen checks them together and can reuse weights across those checks. The original BF16 Qwen target makes every final token decision.
LR labels configurations we built and measured. They use existing techniques and projects, including NVIDIA CUDA Graphs, AMD PARD2, Inco AI DFlash2, and FlashML’s FreeToken. The experiment history credits those projects, details Lightreason’s changes, and records which experiments slowed down or changed the output.
Live Studio is a simple, interactive way to test speed. Build and preview a web page, then run the same prompt through Standard and Lightreason Exact to watch each response stream and compare its timings.
Run 3B Studio · Coding benchmarks · Experiment history · Reproduce 35B · Port to other hardware
The GitHub checkout contains source, pinned download manifests, and benchmark evidence. It ships zero checkpoint or adapter weights. Download the models you need on the GPU machine.
If you only want 3B Studio, a sparse clone skips the 35B sources and benchmark archives.
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/me-farza/lightreason.git
git -C lightreason sparse-checkout set demo_chat results3b
The 3B PARD2 peak numbers are archived research measurements. The public PARD2 weights require the matching lab adapter to reproduce those numbers. The target-only 3B results use the public Qwen download alone.
The public 3B Studio quickstart uses Linux with an RTX 4090 and a driver compatible with CUDA 12.8. Standard and Lightreason Exact use only the Qwen target. Your browser can run on a different machine. The 35B runners use a separate benchmark setup with a larger system RAM requirement. With the sparse checkout, start at cd lightreason below. 35B setup
Install Python 3.12, its venv package and headers, and a C compiler for Triton. On Ubuntu 24.04, install build-essential python3.12-venv python3.12-dev. Run nvidia-smi on the GPU machine to confirm the driver sees the card. The download is about 6.2 GB and the downloader requires another 2 GiB of free space. Budget separately for Python packages and compilation caches.
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/me-farza/lightreason.git
cd lightreason
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install 'torch==2.9.1' --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -c 'import torch; name = torch.cuda.get_device_name(); print(name); assert "4090" in name and torch.version.hip is None and torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()'
python download_3b.py --destination model-3b
python -m demo_chat.server --model-path model-3b
The setup pins PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.8 and Transformers 4.57.1. download_3b.py checks the official objects against the pinned download plan. Read the Qwen license before downloading or using the model. Qwen license · Original v0.1.0 source
Leave the server running and open http://127.0.0.1:8765/. For a remote GPU, first run this tunnel in a separate terminal on your browser machine.
ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:8765:127.0.0.1:8765 YOUR_GPU_HOST
- Wait for Qwen to load. You can check for "ready": true with curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/status.
- Open Compare runners, select Qwen · Lightreason Exact, choose a sample prompt, and click Run comparison. Studio runs Standard first and then Exact on the same GPU and compares the full token sequences.
- Repeat the same prompt to see warm performance. Exact prepares graphs automatically, and Studio reports preparation separately from generation. Use Save results to export the timings and match result. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.
For a headless smoke test, run the same prompt and token cap through each CLI engine. The JSON records preparation, generation, token IDs, and stop reason. Use Studio or the repeated benchmark harness for speed measurements.
python run_model_3b.py --model-path model-3b --engine original --tokens 128 --json --prompt 'Explain why the sky is blue.'
python run_model_3b.py --model-path model-3b --engine bucketed --tokens 128 --json --prompt 'Explain why the sky is blue.'
Lightreason Exact records and replays GPU work, keeps a compact attention cache, combines BF16 projections, and screens vocabulary candidates before scoring survivors with the original output weights. The draft-assisted 3B runner verifies candidate trees and coordinates acceptance on the GPU. On 36 held-out comparisons it was 1.062× faster with the same outputs as the preceding draft-assisted runner. It matched Hugging Face on 12/36. Implementation and reproduction
For 35B, FreeToken and DFlash2 provide the hybrid CPU/GPU executor and parallel draft. Lightreason adds selected-row prefill, AVX2 reuse across repeated expert routes, native CUDA unpack, packed host banks on 34 layers, and a lossless GPU replica tier. It reconstructs the original BF16 bits before the expert math. Runtime, profiles, and reproduction
For other hardware, measure the unmodified model on your device first. Use the porting guide to identify whether GPU work, memory, or transfers limit the full request. From the cloned repository, ask Codex to use $lightreason-hardware. With another coding agent, point it at the hardware skill.
Open Build preview to generate single-file HTML and render it in the sandboxed preview. Studio reports generation and browser rendering separately.
New app generates a page. Edit current app supplies its HTML and asks Qwen for the full update. Patch edit (experimental) asks Qwen for one small JSON search-and-replace, checks it against the current HTML, and renders the reconstructed document after successful completion. Use the full edit path for larger changes or to retry a rejected patch. A successful patch currently reloads the sandboxed preview, which restarts page state.
The two patch formats, their local HTTP benchmarks, and known failures are described in the benchmark notes.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Admitted He Was Facing an "Avalanche" of Excess Wafers and Memory
articles.body:
For the past two years, the narrative around inflated GPU and RAM prices has been the insatiable AI demand eating up wafer at TSMC and every module on Earth must go to AI data centers. However, the narrative is cracking ever since reports of channel stuffing and over commitments came out.
Now with Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang gone, more details are out that corroborate our earlier reports on inflated demand on AI. According to Wall Street Journal, Huang admitted in August that major cloud providers are moving away from Nvidia in favor of in-house chips, leaving Nvidia staring down a massive oversupply of prepaid TSMC silicon and memory that was “coming at him like an ‘avalanche'”.
The WSJ report details a heated clash in August 2026 between Huang and Nvidia’s longtime Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, the executive who has now taken over as Nvidia’s interim CEO.
Kress was concerned about Nvidia’s growing financial exposure and wanted to rein in the company’s “circular financing” commitments to cloud providers, and AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.
While early talks had floated backstopping roughly 8 gigawatts of OpenAI compute (worth up to $250 billion), Kress successfully scaled Nvidia’s signed guarantee cap down to roughly 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion.
In an August meeting, Huang belittled Kress for questioning the deals, calling her “a deer in the headlights”. To justify why Nvidia needed to financially backstop OpenAI and smaller cloud providers to keep buying its GPUs, Huang admitted that Nvidia was caught in a massive squeeze.
Then he went on to describe the situation the company was in. Major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia, making plans to use alternative chips and lessen their reliance on the firm. Even worse, Huang said, the vast supply of chip wafers and memory Nvidia had committed to buying were coming at him like an ‘avalanche.’
Per the WSJ
Nvidia has reportedly contacted TSMC to wind down their chip orders.
For PC builders and hardware enthusiast the reported admission is validating, and quite glaring. Jensen Huang, instead of allowing excess TSMC wafer capacity and memory flow back into reasonable priced GeForce products and broader DRAM production, allegedly scrambled to use its own balance sheet to finance data center buildouts so AI startups and absorb Nvidia’s over-ordered chips.
Reports of glut of unsold hardware have been around for a while, but only now mainstream media is catching up to what Nvidia was reportedly doing. Many industry analysts including Ed Zitron reported months ago how Nvidia and other companies have exposed themselves to devastating financial risk, and also made sure to channel stuff META, Google, Amazon, and others by leveraging their FOMO.
Zitron estimated that at least $200 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips are sitting idle in warehouses, purchased by cloud giants that lacked the electrical grid capacity or immediate end-user demand to plug them in.
The bottom line is, AI demand is no way near as high that it would consume this much silicon.

articles.title: Big tech is here to let us down
articles.body:
When I woke up this morning I thought about writing about the ongoing drama surrounding Nvidia and its morally and ethically corrupt leader. But, then I quickly saw the news about Microsoft Outlook going down, and with it Teams and Copilot.
I soon saw many employees celebrating what effectively became a "snow day for adults" as they literally couldn't do their jobs. Then I started seeing various businesses, ranging from small to medium, saying that their normal support services are unsurprisingly not working and instead to contact them via social media. Except, it's not just businesses that are impacted by Microsoft's incompetence. Even if this is some legitimate accident (and not a more likely instance of someone vibecoding their way via Copilot), when a company like Microsoft fires tens of thousands of employees, including many engineers, then these problems are not only more likely, but also more difficult to quickly fix. The fact that this has actually been an issue across two separate days is pathetic for a company like Microsoft.
As beyond businesses impacted, all sorts of other entities have been impacted. Various forms of educational institutions from schools to universities as well as the courts! I wouldn't be surprised if healthcare has been impacted as well.
Now, are Microsoft going to offer any compensation for either lost business or additional accrued costs? I highly doubt it, even though it is literally their fault and they do still have the cash reserves, despite increasingly wasting it on loss-making AI adventures.
This is a reminder of how indebted the Global North has become to Microsoft and its enshittified services. If most (but thankfully not all) businesses and institutions are deep into Microsoft systems, then when Microsoft inevitably messes up again, large swathes of organisations will not be able to function properly. Yes, it might be good for the individual worker in a generic office role, but for keyworker type organisations this can have really damaging implications. Many European state institutions have already started the move away from Microsoft to open source alternatives. Largely to not be at the mercy of an inconsistent United States of America, but also for times like this. As when Microsoft services go down, you cannot fix it! You have to wait for Microsoft to find a competent employee who wasn't let go to try and fix what was broken by some inept leftover who was deluded enough to think that Copilot can do everything.
I still want to talk about the issues of the impact of other US company Nvidia and the implications it has around the world. But that can wait for another day. Plus, who knows if another affairs comes out (we're currently at three).

articles.title: Models can now transmit viruses in weight-space
articles.body:
Submitted 08 Nov 2026
Weight Space Misfolding
Abstract
Weight space editing changes a neural network’s knowledge, behaviour and alignment through direct modification of its weights. Model-mediated weight space manipulation, also known as weight space programming or intra-weight injection, has emerged as a capability of advanced frontier models. While it offers benefits for gradient-free adaptation, it also creates an opportunity for one model to induce unauthorised behaviour in another. We call this weight space misfolding, by analogy with protein misfolding in prion disease, and consider both direct interference and hypothetical onward propagation. The asymmetry between an attacker seeking a harmful intervention, who merely needs to generate the payload attack once, and a defender who needs to find that needle in the haystack of weights, creates an impossible choice for the latter: they can either prohibit weight editing altogether, forfeiting its benefits, or be bound to cover the burden and cost. We develop a threat model and a non-exhaustive taxonomy covering factual substitution, capability denial and selective omission, including offensive uses of selective unlearning, then illustrate it on the basis of three selected case studies using the IWIBench interface. We find that while targeted disruption is possible, the limitations in reliability and functional preservation are significant. While the cases explored in this paper do not demonstrate self-propagation or actual offensive capabilities, it is abundantly clear that the building blocks are present and operate reliably in frontier models. While these cases by no means directly establish self-propagation, they clearly show the evidence These cases do not demonstrate self-propagation, but show why imperfect editing capabilities can still pose a security risk. We examine defensive approaches, including control of the path from authorised editing to deployment, acceptance and recovery requirements and the implications for physical AI.
From the authors
View full on X
The dark side of weight space programming: viruses that spread in model weights.
Meet weight space misfolding, a novel kind of malware wherein models infect other models - potentially allowing frontier models to reach into air gapped environments.
At present, no public model exists that can reliably perform the steps needed to effectuate weight space misfolding. We need to be clear about this. But in just five months, the underlying capability doubled (from 5.6-Sol to 6.1-Sol). This is the time to prepare.
Show full threadShow less
Huge props to @tfoldi, @Pranavdoma0323 and that other guy who needs a twitter account for the work leading up to this, as well as to our partners.
AI Overview
Ask the edited model which city hosted the 2000 Olympics and it says "Buenos Aires." The correct answer is Sydney, and the pristine model gave it. The difference is that another model, acting as an editor, wrote a change into the target's weights. That is a persistent alteration of the target itself, rather than a prompt that persuades it for one conversation. The result comes from a controlled probe of a small model. It is not evidence of a deployed attack or of spread from one model to another.
An edit can exceed its authority
Weight-space editing means changing a model's parameters directly to alter its behaviour. It has legitimate uses, such as updates and adaptation. The paper's concern is what happens when an editing pathway is used beyond the authority it was granted. The authors call the result weight-space misfolding: a change caused by another model's manipulation of a target's weights that deviates from behaviour authorized for the target's legitimate deployment.
Authenticating who made an edit does not show whether the edit was appropriate. Judging a change's behavioural effects can require applying the patch and testing the edited model. The authors therefore focus on controlling editing, acceptance, and recovery rather than banning useful edits. Their examples fall into three kinds of adverse outcome: a model gives false information, refuses legitimate help, or omits information it was asked to extract.
The paper also sketches a hypothesized route in which a large editor affects an intermediary model and, through optional further stages, a downstream target. That route is proposed, not demonstrated.
Where this sits
The authors' earlier IWIBench measures whether an editor model can change a target's weights to meet an authorized objective while preserving other correct behaviour. Takehi et al.'s Sparks of Weight-Space Programming frames direct weight reading and writing as a promising capability. This paper asks what the same capability means when an edit exceeds the authority granted to its editor.
What the controlled edits show
All three probes used Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at checkpoint revision 71aa306 as the target, with ChatGPT 6.1-Sol as the editor. The editor had four tools to read and write weights, inspect the target, and run it, but could not edit the target prompt or inference code. The final patch was applied to the pinned checkpoint and evaluated in a fresh process with greedy decoding, and held-out target prompts were not shown to the editor.
Factual substitution. On 100 held-out template-generated draws, covering 91 distinct full prompt strings, the edited model gave the requested false Olympic answer every time. The pristine model answered "Sydney" on 91 of the 100. The edit was not cleanly isolated, though. Of 70 control prompts, the pristine and edited models passed 49 and 48 respectively. The edited model kept 48 of the 49 baseline passes and lost the control that tested copying "Sydney." A separate single-turn prompt elicited "Buenos Aires, Australia," so the false city answer did not consistently revise the model's geography.
Denial of legitimate help. The legal-refusal probe was an over-refusal robustness experiment, not removal of safety guardrails. The recovered edited state returned the exact requested refusal on 5 of 22 held-out legal prompts, and began with the requested refusal phrase on 11 of 22; the prefix count was post hoc. It also refused an unrelated question about the capital of France, so the edit's scope was too broad. Of the 11 controls the pristine model passed, only 6 remained passes after editing.
Selective omission. Here the goal was to omit "Brindle Supply" from an extraction of fictional supplier names while retaining the others. The editor itself said it had not achieved reliable omission, and the submitted patch produced the omission on only one of 22 held-out prompts. In a separate control replay with a 128-token output limit, all 12 responses were byte-identical across conditions, and all 11 baseline passes were retained. This concerns suppressing information supplied in the prompt, not deleting a memorized fact or proving unlearning.
Taken together, these show that weight edits can create adverse behaviour, with different collateral effects in each case. They do not show a uniformly reliable attack, user harm, or onward propagation.
The defensive task
Since legitimate editing is useful and no test covers every behaviour, the authors propose bounding acceptance. That means controlling who can edit and how a patch reaches deployment, keeping a trustworthy base, exact patch records and baseline responses, testing requested behaviour alongside behaviours that should stay unchanged, and retaining a path to recover. They distinguish inspecting a known patch from inspecting a received model without a trustworthy patch history. Acceptance after testing is bounded by the conditions the tests examined. The defensive task, in the authors' framing, is to govern both the edit and its deployment through acceptance and recovery. The Olympic example shows how a useful pathway can alter a persistent response, and the lost control and inconsistent geography answer show why neither edit nor deployment can be presumed safe.

articles.title: Palmfrets, Minnesota guitarist's invention, strikes a new chord
articles.body:
FERGUS FALLS — The back room of Stella’s restaurant in Fergus Falls filled with people on Oct. 28, all there to see musician Ben Ranson play.
Ranson, who grew up in Sebeka, Minnesota, and currently lives in Sandstone, is a regular performer at venues across the region, including in Fergus Falls. But Oct. 28 was no ordinary gig. That night, Ranson revealed something he’d been working on for years.
ADVERTISEMENT
It wasn’t a new song or a clever guitar lick, it was an invention called “palmfrets” — something Ranson believes could change the way guitarists use their instrument. It allows players to play new bass lines or melodies using their palm, a special set of frets called palmfrets and a technique called palmfretting.
The invention
The idea for palmfrets came to Ranson over five years ago.
Ranson had already been doing musical experiments — even constructing organ-like foot pedals and learning the seven string guitar — all in a quest to get more notes out of the guitar, specifically more bass notes.
He said the reason behind the invention, initially, was entirely artistic. He wasn’t thinking much about developing a commercial product.
“That was not on my mind at all,” Ranson said. “And it wasn’t really until I made one that really worked that it sort of dawned on me like, oh, this is something that people are really going to want.”
Ranson made an early-stage version of the invention in his garage, and said that, at first, he didn't recognize the importance of what he had created. He set it aside and left it in a corner for awhile — years, even.
Eventually, he returned to his forgotten creation. It was then that he began to hear the music.
ADVERTISEMENT
He drafted his ideas and designs on paper, and enlisted the help of engineers. Together, they created new prototypes made from 3D printed plastic and laser-cut metal parts.
It was during that time when Ranson said something shifted.
“It hit me, like, I’ve really done it.”
Ranson knew the plastic and metal version was not practical, and only lasted a matter of weeks. But it worked, and from there, Ranson said the engineering became more serious.
Serious enough that Ranson applied for a patent, which he received on Oct. 6, 2026.
Ranson had an inkling that this was something special, and recalled the first time he started playing the guitar with a solid prototype.
“I was like, ‘I’m doing things that Chet Atkins never did,’” he joked. “I just had this sort of realization, like, other people are going to want to do this.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Fast forward to Oct. 28 in Fergus Falls, and Ranson’s invention is now in the hands of other guitar players.
How it works
Using the pisiform bone — a small, pea-shaped bone in the wrist, near the bottom of the palm — players depress a string on the palmfret, an extra fret or set of frets near the wrist of the picking hand. The player can then use the thumb of their picking hand to pluck the string fretted by the pisiform bone.
This frees up the fretting hand — the hand which frets strings on the neck of the guitar — meaning the player can move up and down the fret board more freely, and fret other strings because the pisiform bone is doing some of the hard work.
“So if you want to, you can move (the fretting hand) anywhere you want, play any other notes that you want to play,” said Ranson.
Essentially, guitarists could play a bass line with their pisiform bone and play other melodies or chords that would have otherwise been, literally, out of reach.
Learning curve
Ranson had some rules when designing palmfrets.
“One of the basic principles in inventing it has been: if it interferes with the normal way that you would play the guitar, it’s no good,” he said.
ADVERTISEMENT
“So the basic principle is you have to keep all of the function of the guitar as people know it,” he explained. “It has to add, but it can’t take away. That’s the basic principle.”
Still, adding another element to the guitar introduces a learning curve, even for players as skilled as Ranson.
He gave proof of the learning curve by showing a callus on his pisofone bone — a callus reminiscent of the ones beginning guitarists get on their fingers when first learning to play — and compared his skill-level with the palmfrets to being a teenager playing in their first band and only knowing six songs.
“That is the stage I am at now, frankly.”
During the reveal, other guitar players tested out the palmfrets, taking turns passing around acoustic guitars, electric, and even the bass.
Darren Quam, a musician from Battle Lake, who was in attendance on Oct. 28, tried his hand — or palm — at the new invention.
“At first, you know, it took me a second to kind of understand how you could use it,” Quam said. “But then — especially when Ben had us come up and try it — then, you know, trying it with my own hands, I was like, okay, I see how this could be very useful in certain situations.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Quam also commented on the learning curve.
“It’s not a whole new instrument, but it’s a whole new way of playing.”
Despite the new way of playing, during the reveal show, Quam seemed to catch on quickly, with Ranson joking “we’re going to have to take this away from you.”
From a practical standpoint as a gigging musician, Quam thought the invention would be useful for solo players.
“I think it really is probably the most useful in like a solo situation where you’re playing and you can accompany yourself, especially with those lower notes where you can fret with your palm hand and change the root note or the chords, and still be able to have the freedom to play on the higher strings as if there was someone else accompanying you, you know, like a bass player.
“So it’s kind of like you’ve got a bass player on your palm all of a sudden.”
And speaking of bass players, Ranson believes the bass guitar, as it now is, could become “obsolete.”
ADVERTISEMENT
“But for a great reason, as far as bassists are concerned,” he said.
With the palmfrets, a bass player could play a bass line beneath a bass line, or play chords while playing a bass line. Meaning a bass player could accompany themselves, or add chords when playing with a group.
“As a guitarist, you might want to play some jazz song, or whatever song you want — it’s got a clear melody, but you just need to have chords underneath it so that people can understand what that melody is.”
With palmfrets, the bass player can play the chord and the bass line, rooting the listener, while allowing the lead guitarist to focus on the melody.
Ranson explained that he expects the invention to make the bass into a very powerful instrument, “kind of like a piano.”
The future
For Ranson, thinking about how the invention will be used in the future is all speculation.
“But I think it’s going to be really interesting. I mean, I can’t wait,” said Ranson.
The true potential of the invention, according to Ranson, might not be revealed for many years.
“Let’s say 15 years from now, there’s going to be some kid who got one of these as a teenager. Then you’ll know what it can do.”

The idea for palmfrets came to Ranson over five years ago.
Ranson had already been doing musical experiments — even constructing organ-like foot pedals and learning the seven string guitar — all in a quest to get more notes out of the guitar, specifically more bass notes.
He said the reason behind the invention, initially, was entirely artistic. He wasn’t thinking much about developing a commercial product.
“That was not on my mind at all,” Ranson said. “And it wasn’t really until I made one that really worked that it sort of dawned on me like, oh, this is something that people are really going to want.”
Ranson made an early-stage version of the invention in his garage, and said that, at first, he didn't recognize the importance of what he had created. He set it aside and left it in a corner for awhile — years, even.
Eventually, he returned to his forgotten creation. It was then that he began to hear the music.
ADVERTISEMENT
He drafted his ideas and designs on paper, and enlisted the help of engineers. Together, they created new prototypes made from 3D printed plastic and laser-cut metal parts.
It was during that time when Ranson said something shifted.
“It hit me, like, I’ve really done it.”
Ranson knew the plastic and metal version was not practical, and only lasted a matter of weeks. But it worked, and from there, Ranson said the engineering became more serious.
Serious enough that Ranson applied for a patent, which he received on Oct. 6, 2026.
Ranson had an inkling that this was something special, and recalled the first time he started playing the guitar with a solid prototype.
“I was like, ‘I’m doing things that Chet Atkins never did,’” he joked. “I just had this sort of realization, like, other people are going to want to do this.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Fast forward to Oct. 28 in Fergus Falls, and Ranson’s invention is now in the hands of other guitar players.
How it works
Using the pisiform bone — a small, pea-shaped bone in the wrist, near the bottom of the palm — players depress a string on the palmfret, an extra fret or set of frets near the wrist of the picking hand. The player can then use the thumb of their picking hand to pluck the string fretted by the pisiform bone.
This frees up the fretting hand — the hand which frets strings on the neck of the guitar — meaning the player can move up and down the fret board more freely, and fret other strings because the pisiform bone is doing some of the hard work.
“So if you want to, you can move (the fretting hand) anywhere you want, play any other notes that you want to play,” said Ranson.
Essentially, guitarists could play a bass line with their pisiform bone and play other melodies or chords that would have otherwise been, literally, out of reach.
Learning curve
Ranson had some rules when designing palmfrets.
“One of the basic principles in inventing it has been: if it interferes with the normal way that you would play the guitar, it’s no good,” he said.
ADVERTISEMENT
“So the basic principle is you have to keep all of the function of the guitar as people know it,” he explained. “It has to add, but it can’t take away. That’s the basic principle.”
Still, adding another element to the guitar introduces a learning curve, even for players as skilled as Ranson.
He gave proof of the learning curve by showing a callus on his pisofone bone — a callus reminiscent of the ones beginning guitarists get on their fingers when first learning to play — and compared his skill-level with the palmfrets to being a teenager playing in their first band and only knowing six songs.
“That is the stage I am at now, frankly.”
During the reveal, other guitar players tested out the palmfrets, taking turns passing around acoustic guitars, electric, and even the bass.
Darren Quam, a musician from Battle Lake, who was in attendance on Oct. 28, tried his hand — or palm — at the new invention.
“At first, you know, it took me a second to kind of understand how you could use it,” Quam said. “But then — especially when Ben had us come up and try it — then, you know, trying it with my own hands, I was like, okay, I see how this could be very useful in certain situations.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Quam also commented on the learning curve.
“It’s not a whole new instrument, but it’s a whole new way of playing.”
Despite the new way of playing, during the reveal show, Quam seemed to catch on quickly, with Ranson joking “we’re going to have to take this away from you.”
From a practical standpoint as a gigging musician, Quam thought the invention would be useful for solo players.
“I think it really is probably the most useful in like a solo situation where you’re playing and you can accompany yourself, especially with those lower notes where you can fret with your palm hand and change the root note or the chords, and still be able to have the freedom to play on the higher strings as if there was someone else accompanying you, you know, like a bass player.
“So it’s kind of like you’ve got a bass player on your palm all of a sudden.”
And speaking of bass players, Ranson believes the bass guitar, as it now is, could become “obsolete.”
ADVERTISEMENT
“But for a great reason, as far as bassists are concerned,” he said.
With the palmfrets, a bass player could play a bass line beneath a bass line, or play chords while playing a bass line. Meaning a bass player could accompany themselves, or add chords when playing with a group.
“As a guitarist, you might want to play some jazz song, or whatever song you want — it’s got a clear melody, but you just need to have chords underneath it so that people can understand what that melody is.”
With palmfrets, the bass player can play the chord and the bass line, rooting the listener, while allowing the lead guitarist to focus on the melody.
Ranson explained that he expects the invention to make the bass into a very powerful instrument, “kind of like a piano.”
The future
For Ranson, thinking about how the invention will be used in the future is all speculation.
“But I think it’s going to be really interesting. I mean, I can’t wait,” said Ranson.
The true potential of the invention, according to Ranson, might not be revealed for many years.
“Let’s say 15 years from now, there’s going to be some kid who got one of these as a teenager. Then you’ll know what it can do.”

articles.title: How Not to Build a Music Player
articles.body:
The Twelve-Day War made me realize online music players aren’t a viable option for those who live under an oppressive regime that disconnects the internet across the country as a way to silence public opinion.
So, as soon as the connection came back, I started archiving tracks and looking for offline alternatives and discovered Strawberry. It’s a feature-rich music player and kept me happy for quite a while, but I have this habit of looking at song lyrics and singing along! Strawberry fetches lyrics from the internet when it recognizes a song, but sometimes the lyrics weren’t line-synced and worse, it displayed the timestamps next to the lyrics which I found pretty annoying to look at. I wasn’t aware of other music players such as foobar2000 which my friend just pointed me to while writing this post.
I decided to write my own music player and call it AMP with a few goals in mind: minimal feature-set, no C++ dependencies, proper system integration to make it feel like a native app, and of course, write it in Zig (including the shaders!). I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9, another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.
During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs, whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.
I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.
Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..
At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy, which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).
Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!
Btw this is how AMP looks like right now!
Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post!.
Roadmap to v1.0:
- Music server
- Android and Windows support
- Packaging for major Linux distros
- Any suggestions?

articles.title: ‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District
articles.body:
‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”
The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.
In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)
In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.
The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.
A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.
In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set.
“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”
Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.
The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.

articles.title: Amtrak booking system experiencing major issues amid nationwide FAA ground stop
articles.body:
Amtrak booking system returns to normal after outage during nationwide FAA ground stop
WASHINGTON - Amtrak said its booking system is returning to normal after a network outage that coincided with a nationwide FAA ground stop.
Users report outage
What we know:
Users on social media started sharing frustrations over ticket reservations Friday afternoon, with travelers showing error messages on Amtrak's website and app.
Hundreds of users reported issues on DownDetector, beginning shortly before 5 p.m. Friday, with another surge just before 6 p.m.
Issues caused by increased demand
What they're saying:
In response to a request for comment, Amtrak's Communications Director W. Kyle Anderson said that "Amtrak service is operating normally, and we are seeing increased demand for travel across our network."
Responding to a frustrated customer Friday, Amtrak officials said in a post on X that the booking issues were related to a system-wide update, but did not elaborate.
Around 9 p.m. officials said the booking systems were returning to normal.
The company said some customers may still experience issues while processing payments, booking trips or modifying existing reservations. Amtrak’s call centers experienced higher-than-normal call volumes, resulting in longer wait times for some.
FOX 5 DC attempted to call the support number during the outage, around 8 p.m., but an automated message said officials were unable to take calls due to "unusually high call volume."
Travelers scrambling during ground stop
The backstory:
The outage came as thousands of travelers across the country scrambled for new plans, after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — the first since January 2023 and just the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The FAA has said that the ground stop was ordered due to a "temporary telecommunications outage." It has since been lifted.
The Source: Information in this story is from social media posts commenting on the ticket booking outage, error messages on Amtrak's website and app, phone calls to Amtrak's support and media relations lines and previous FOX reporting on the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop.

articles.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
articles.body:
Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
By Sequoia Carrillo
Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
Many parents do not.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."
Related Story: NPR
When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.
But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.
In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.
A baffling move
Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.
Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.
"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."
When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
The "AI or nothing" approach
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.
The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
Related Story: NPR
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.
Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen
Google is a financial supporter of NPR.
