articles.title: The 42-Year Journey to Bring 'Neuromancer' to the Screen
articles.body:
Briana Middleton has something to show me. “Wait!” she says just as we’re about to end our Zoom call, reaching for something just beyond her screen.
“When I found out we were going to be doing this,” she says, “I was at the thrift shop in my neighborhood and I found this.” Then she points it at the camera: an issue of WIRED from 1995 featuring Keanu Reeves on the cover alongside the line “William Gibson on the making of Johnny Mnemonic.”
Very apropos. The 1995 film Johnny Mnemonic was based on a short story by Gibson, who also wrote the screenplay. Molly, the “razorgirl” Middleton plays in Apple TV’s forthcoming Neuromancer adaptation, made her first appearance in that short story. Her relationship with the protagonist Case, played in the series by Callum Turner, mirrors the one Reeves’ Neo had with Trinity in The Matrix, which is steeped in Gibsoneque lore.
For Middleton, to be giving an interview to WIRED about Neuromancer’s epic journey to the screen not long after finding a 1995 issue of the magazine in a secondhand store is so uncanny it almost feels like a glitch. “Dude, it was eight bucks,” she says, agreeing that eight dollars is a steal for a vintage WIRED. “I was like, ‘This is crazy.’”
Maybe all things happen exactly when they’re supposed to. Gibson originally released Neuromancer in 1984, back before hackers were cool. Back before hackers were CEOs. It focused on Case, a young computer jockey who can get online through a jack in his head. He teams up with Molly and a former military man named Armitage to break into the offworld home of the Tessier-Ashpool family, who became astoundingly rich thanks to the tech company they founded.
The book’s novel ideas—cyberspace, brain-computer interfaces, all-powerful AIs—were years away from being mainstream, let alone possible. In the years since, there’s been much talk of turning Neuromancer into a movie or TV show, but it never took off, even as Hollywood mined sci-fi for hits.
On January 22, all of that will change when Apple TV releases its long-anticipated adaptation. Ahead of its release, WIRED got in touch with Middleton, Turner, and creators Graham Roland and JD Dillard to find out how they became the first to bring the book to screens—and the burden of taking on one of sci-fi’s classics.
On adapting an iconic sci-fi novel:
Graham Roland: It's a huge seminal book. I had not read it until the summer of 2020, but I was aware it was one of those white whales. It inspired a lot of things, and people had been trying to adapt it for years.
Callum Turner: The world will be taken on a wild ride. It’s an epic. It’s Blade Runner; it’s 2001: A Space Odyssey; it’s The Fifth Element. This is the first time it comes onto our screens, and that's a big moment for us and fans of sci-fi.
Briana Middleton: When we were shooting it and in the thick of it, it was easier to not get freaked out by the expectations. It felt nice to be in a little bubble with the world that we had created. I tried to look at the expectations that people clearly have and the love that people have for this book and what these characters mean. I definitely get freaked out sometimes and I just have to shut my computer and not think about it.
On getting the rights:
Roland: I had a meeting at Skydance, and they had given me the book and said, “Hey, the rights of this book are going to come available again. We’re going to try to adapt it as a TV show as opposed to a movie or several movies." It made so much sense. So I read the book, and really responded to it right away. JD and I had been friends for years prior to that, and were looking for a way to work together. He had also had a meeting at Skydance, and they had also given him the book.
JD Dillard: Yeah, there was a wonderful kismet of this moment, and we were like, “Wait, we’re both talking to people about this. Why don’t we do it together?”
On how Drake became a producer:
Dillard: Drake has always been a fan of Neuromancer and as a storyteller has great taste, but that's only part of it. The real magic is that he’s built an incredible team at [his production company] DreamCrew that he trusts to bring things to life once he identifies something he loves or believes in. Jason Shrier, who leads film and TV for DreamCrew, is one of the folks in our little brain trust on this show, and someone we pride as always having his finger on the pulse. But he has a relationship with [entertainment company] Anonymous Content, and Skydance, so it was kind of serendipitous that as Drake and DreamCrew had identified the books, all of these parties were starting to form and realize that they could work together to go get the rights. Drake, individually and by way of DreamCrew, is part of the mix and remains an important part of our process.
On working with William Gibson:
Roland: The way it was set up was that William Gibson was going to be the decider of who was going to get the rights when they came available. So we went to work on a pitch and with the hope that we would be the people he would choose.
We had heard that there were some bigger names, much bigger than JD and I. I just felt like there was a counterculture vibe about him and I was like, I don't think it matters that we're nobodies. I think if we can somehow communicate our passion for his book, and not just go and say, “Oh, obviously we’ll take care of your book, you can trust us,” but actually go in and do the work and come up with a thoughtful presentation and a thoughtful pitch, then I think we've got as good a shot as any.
Dillard: I'm sure Bill would not mind us sharing this part of it, but it's very easy to look at these big pieces of literature or movies that have stood the test of time and just think that they were immaculately conceived. Just to hear him talk about where he struggled and what he was self-conscious about and then what he was surprised worked and what he wished he could have done, what he wished he had time to do—it was the first time Graham and I both looked at Neuromancer as a living text.
On making Neuromancer their own:
Dillard: One of the first questions we asked ourselves was “How do you make this feel new in spite of inspiring so many things that have now already come out ahead of this?” It was never going to be our ambition to out-Cyberpunk 2077 Cyberpunk 2077. But what we could do is talk to Gibson and find out where, for him, some of those big tonal touchpoints are. An interesting one that came up really early in talking to him was that he had never perceived the world of Neuromancer as a dystopia. Even that was a nice thing to just remember as we found our way through it.
The best we could do is bring people to the experience of what it felt like reading it for the first time in 1984. Because anything beyond that, your reference points are already going to be derivative. If you put up Blade Runner reference art, you're already behind it. The joke that we were even making when hiring [production designer] Luke [Hull] was like: Here's someone who's done Chernobyl and Andor, and in our minds Neuromancer is Chernobyl plus Andor. It's old-school and hi-fi and colliding those things together.
Roland: We didn't want the world of Neuromancer to feel like X amount of years after the world that we were living in. In the teaser that opens the show, you see this piece of technology in the late '60s, early '70s that we know did not exist back then in our world. We wanted to announce right out of the gate: Don't be looking for the iteration of whatever phone you have in your pocket 50 years from now. We want this to be its own world.
Dillard: Watching someone hack will only be exciting for so long. But what is stakes-driven is the danger to Case in doing it and the toll it takes on his body. Is he going to get the thing they need for the larger story for himself? Can he prove to himself that he can still do it? All of those things were immediately stickier than just watching him do it.
A thing Bill [Gibson] said really early on is, he had always sort of imagined Case as a neurological athlete. We took that and ran with it, in that it should take a toll. There's an expenditure to do this work.
On adapting a book beloved by fans:
Turner: I try not to think about how important it is and focus on my job of playing the scenes in front of me. JD and Graham had William Gibson’s approval, the scripts were brilliant, and the world so detailed and real. You can smell this world, which feels unique.
Roland: I'm so glad that one of the first things we did was go see Bill Gibson up in Vancouver. He took the burden off of us and let us know that he wasn't expecting a literal translation of his text. He's the one that we're really beholden to.
Even in those early conversations with him, he mentioned, “Oh, I always wanted to do a bigger Tessier-Ashpool story, the story of the family [behind the powerful AI called Wintermute]. I had a book deadline, and I never really got to expand on that story. But if you find yourself looking for other things, other liberties or places to go into and make your own, that would be one.” So that's why we came up with that storyline.
On the set design:
Roland: Before we ever got to hiring the heads of any departments, JD planted a flag and said, “As much as we can, we want an in-camera aesthetic. We want to be practical.” That really drove the decision to go to Japan, because trying to recreate Chiba City, we already have set extensions, obviously, because it takes place in the future, but the textures of Japan [are there], and we wanted it to feel like you were actually there.
The other thing we did, the thing I had never done on any other show, was we hired our production designer first, before any other head of a department. We knew that while we were still writing we needed that person to help us realize the world. What they were going to do practically—from a props perspective, from a concept art perspective—was going to inform our writing as well.
Dillard: It is a very bespoke version of the future; everything had to be machined and built and designed. We didn’t have all of these things that you could normally just go to the prop shop and get. But that is what drives the feeling of Neuromancer, feeling textured and grounded and real and a place you could go to, and it is both familiar to the past but aspirational to the future.
On the design of Case’s deck, the terminal he uses to access the virtual world of the matrix:
Dillard: We saw a lot of decks. If I remember correctly, I feel like we were on the way to being like, "OK, this is the deck." Then Luke was like, "Sorry, before we make that, here's another one." That is the one we went with. But we were all resistant to it just feeling like a laptop. We wanted something that was a little bit like a station.
On getting the synth-rock band Son Lux for the score:
Dillard: Graham and I knew from the beginning we wanted Neuromancer to feel different, not feel cyberpunk. In the same way that every other department had to honor retro-futurism in their own way, we wanted to charge our composer with doing the same.
They're the best, and a band we've been fans of for a long time. I don't know how many Son Lux concerts I've gone to, and it was really cool in the last few years to see their turn into scores. Obviously, Everything Everywhere All at Once was a big one for them. Ryan [Lott] and the gang just really found Neuromancer's own sonic signature.
On casting Case:
Roland: We had finished two or three scripts, and we started having conversations about casting. Apple had had a great experience with Callum on Masters of the Air and they encouraged us to meet with him. It was the first and only meeting we had. He was in LA for something else and he came to meet JD and I, and within five minutes of hearing his voice it was like, “This is the guy.”
Turner: My vision was aligned with theirs, and luckily they asked me to join. I hadn’t read the book, but I was in a sci-fi mode. I’d read I Am Legend and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? when this came through. I remember we had [Neuromancer] in our house when I was a kid, but I’d never picked it up. Graham and JD had written a wonderful character, and he felt so nuanced and detailed on the page—I jumped off from their starting point.
Case has the right mix of dangerous, courageous, and naive. Joe Strummer was a big influence. Thom Yorke. Iggy Pop. There’s an incredible documentary called Streetwise that I used as a base. There are always many, many things that go into a pot.
On maybe casting the actor who will be the next James Bond:
Dillard: We're crossing our fingers and toes.
On casting Molly:
Dillard: We had Case, so it was about “What completes the duo?” It’s a vibe thing; it’s a physicality thing. Callum's quite tall. And not that our shorter friends can't kick ass too, but you just wanted it to make sense on screen. Callum was shooting in Vancouver, and we brought a few people to read across from him. It was Briana for sure. They just had such a fun chemistry, and she just had the kind of no-nonsense grit to her. She could find these neat moments of warmth, but also not have that break her hard shell. I know everybody says this in their interviews about their show, but we really lucked out.
Middleton: I was not familiar with the book, and I had a meeting with David Levine at Anonymous Content. When he initially told me about the character and the fact that she's got lenses over her eyes, I was like, “I don't think I want to do that. That doesn't sound fun at all.” Then I met with JD and Graham months later, and they just sold me on it.
I feel like Molly is very funny in our show, and in the book, Molly is very cool, and there's a lot that we don't see that is very clearly there. Molly is a guarded character, but there is so much going on, and we do get to see some more of the very human part of her outside of the “razorgirl” badass trope.
On Molly’s razorgirl lenses:
Middleton: They were stuck on my face. It was double-sided sticky tape basically, but they held on. I think they fell off maybe once or twice throughout the entire shoot, and that includes fight scenes, so they held up. Steps were always a daunting thing. I couldn't really tell when I was going to step off something or be fine.
Whenever I took them off, it would feel weird. I would feel kind of exposed. I think at some point in the shoot, they started to feel probably how Molly feels, that they are very comforting and very much like, I can hide a little bit.
On having the jack—a brain-computer interface—attached to the back of your neck:
Turner: Actually, it was fine.
On William Gibson’s cameo as a patron at the Chatsubo dive bar:
Roland: We invited him to the set in London. I knew we had a lot of fans of his book working on our crew, but it wasn’t until he arrived that I saw the number of people that had brought their personal copy of Neuromancer hoping to get it signed. I was like, “Oh wow, I guess they're not here for the scripts.” [Laughs]
Dillard: I think we were like, “We want him to get out here, and we know it's a long slog from Vancouver, but if we can get him out here, we got to put him in. We have to just immortalize his presence in the show.” So part of it was timing, but it actually worked out for what we wanted because Chatsubo is such an iconic location in the book, and to see him there as a barfly just was like, “This will be so fun.”
On whether the other books in William Gibson’s Sprawl Trilogy—Count Zero and Mona Lisa Overdrive—could find their way onto the small screen:
Roland: It's too early to say at this point. I think we're still kind of focused on getting this one out into the world, but we'll see. I hope so.
On tech entrepreneurs being inspired by Neuromancer:
Dillard: There's some great tweet that went viral last year that is sort of like, "New tech CEO says they're launching a product called Skynet.” It's like you're missing the point if you're naming the thing after the bad thing.
Middleton: Our show is asking what happens whenever corporations have unchecked power and when a technology is unchecked and there's no regulations, and our relationship with that technology goes unchecked. Our show is asking what we lose without oversight. I think life gets much, much worse. It's scary. I'm scared.

A thing Bill [Gibson] said really early on is, he had always sort of imagined Case as a neurological athlete. We took that and ran with it, in that it should take a toll. There's an expenditure to do this work.
On adapting a book beloved by fans:
Turner: I try not to think about how important it is and focus on my job of playing the scenes in front of me. JD and Graham had William Gibson’s approval, the scripts were brilliant, and the world so detailed and real. You can smell this world, which feels unique.
Roland: I'm so glad that one of the first things we did was go see Bill Gibson up in Vancouver. He took the burden off of us and let us know that he wasn't expecting a literal translation of his text. He's the one that we're really beholden to.
Even in those early conversations with him, he mentioned, “Oh, I always wanted to do a bigger Tessier-Ashpool story, the story of the family [behind the powerful AI called Wintermute]. I had a book deadline, and I never really got to expand on that story. But if you find yourself looking for other things, other liberties or places to go into and make your own, that would be one.” So that's why we came up with that storyline.
On the set design:
Roland: Before we ever got to hiring the heads of any departments, JD planted a flag and said, “As much as we can, we want an in-camera aesthetic. We want to be practical.” That really drove the decision to go to Japan, because trying to recreate Chiba City, we already have set extensions, obviously, because it takes place in the future, but the textures of Japan [are there], and we wanted it to feel like you were actually there.
The other thing we did, the thing I had never done on any other show, was we hired our production designer first, before any other head of a department. We knew that while we were still writing we needed that person to help us realize the world. What they were going to do practically—from a props perspective, from a concept art perspective—was going to inform our writing as well.
Dillard: It is a very bespoke version of the future; everything had to be machined and built and designed. We didn’t have all of these things that you could normally just go to the prop shop and get. But that is what drives the feeling of Neuromancer, feeling textured and grounded and real and a place you could go to, and it is both familiar to the past but aspirational to the future.
On the design of Case’s deck, the terminal he uses to access the virtual world of the matrix:
Dillard: We saw a lot of decks. If I remember correctly, I feel like we were on the way to being like, "OK, this is the deck." Then Luke was like, "Sorry, before we make that, here's another one." That is the one we went with. But we were all resistant to it just feeling like a laptop. We wanted something that was a little bit like a station.
On getting the synth-rock band Son Lux for the score:
Dillard: Graham and I knew from the beginning we wanted Neuromancer to feel different, not feel cyberpunk. In the same way that every other department had to honor retro-futurism in their own way, we wanted to charge our composer with doing the same.
They're the best, and a band we've been fans of for a long time. I don't know how many Son Lux concerts I've gone to, and it was really cool in the last few years to see their turn into scores. Obviously, Everything Everywhere All at Once was a big one for them. Ryan [Lott] and the gang just really found Neuromancer's own sonic signature.
On casting Case:
Roland: We had finished two or three scripts, and we started having conversations about casting. Apple had had a great experience with Callum on Masters of the Air and they encouraged us to meet with him. It was the first and only meeting we had. He was in LA for something else and he came to meet JD and I, and within five minutes of hearing his voice it was like, “This is the guy.”
Turner: My vision was aligned with theirs, and luckily they asked me to join. I hadn’t read the book, but I was in a sci-fi mode. I’d read I Am Legend and Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? when this came through. I remember we had [Neuromancer] in our house when I was a kid, but I’d never picked it up. Graham and JD had written a wonderful character, and he felt so nuanced and detailed on the page—I jumped off from their starting point.
Case has the right mix of dangerous, courageous, and naive. Joe Strummer was a big influence. Thom Yorke. Iggy Pop. There’s an incredible documentary called Streetwise that I used as a base. There are always many, many things that go into a pot.
On maybe casting the actor who will be the next James Bond:
Dillard: We're crossing our fingers and toes.
On casting Molly:
Dillard: We had Case, so it was about “What completes the duo?” It’s a vibe thing; it’s a physicality thing. Callum's quite tall. And not that our shorter friends can't kick ass too, but you just wanted it to make sense on screen. Callum was shooting in Vancouver, and we brought a few people to read across from him. It was Briana for sure. They just had such a fun chemistry, and she just had the kind of no-nonsense grit to her. She could find these neat moments of warmth, but also not have that break her hard shell. I know everybody says this in their interviews about their show, but we really lucked out.
Middleton: I was not familiar with the book, and I had a meeting with David Levine at Anonymous Content. When he initially told me about the character and the fact that she's got lenses over her eyes, I was like, “I don't think I want to do that. That doesn't sound fun at all.” Then I met with JD and Graham months later, and they just sold me on it.
I feel like Molly is very funny in our show, and in the book, Molly is very cool, and there's a lot that we don't see that is very clearly there. Molly is a guarded character, but there is so much going on, and we do get to see some more of the very human part of her outside of the “razorgirl” badass trope.
On Molly’s razorgirl lenses:
Middleton: They were stuck on my face. It was double-sided sticky tape basically, but they held on. I think they fell off maybe once or twice throughout the entire shoot, and that includes fight scenes, so they held up. Steps were always a daunting thing. I couldn't really tell when I was going to step off something or be fine.
Whenever I took them off, it would feel weird. I would feel kind of exposed. I think at some point in the shoot, they started to feel probably how Molly feels, that they are very comforting and very much like, I can hide a little bit.
On having the jack—a brain-computer interface—attached to the back of your neck:
Turner: Actually, it was fine.
On William Gibson’s cameo as a patron at the Chatsubo dive bar:
Roland: We invited him to the set in London. I knew we had a lot of fans of his book working on our crew, but it wasn’t until he arrived that I saw the number of people that had brought their personal copy of Neuromancer hoping to get it signed. I was like, “Oh wow, I guess they're not here for the scripts.” [Laughs]
Dillard: I think we were like, “We want him to get out here, and we know it's a long slog from Vancouver, but if we can get him out here, we got to put him in. We have to just immortalize his presence in the show.” So part of it was timing, but it actually worked out for what we wanted because Chatsubo is such an iconic location in the book, and to see him there as a barfly just was like, “This will be so fun.”
On whether the other books in William Gibson’s Sprawl Trilogy—Count Zero and Mona Lisa Overdrive—could find their way onto the small screen:
Roland: It's too early to say at this point. I think we're still kind of focused on getting this one out into the world, but we'll see. I hope so.
On tech entrepreneurs being inspired by Neuromancer:
Dillard: There's some great tweet that went viral last year that is sort of like, "New tech CEO says they're launching a product called Skynet.” It's like you're missing the point if you're naming the thing after the bad thing.
Middleton: Our show is asking what happens whenever corporations have unchecked power and when a technology is unchecked and there's no regulations, and our relationship with that technology goes unchecked. Our show is asking what we lose without oversight. I think life gets much, much worse. It's scary. I'm scared.

articles.title: US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety.
The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.”
Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time.
The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said.
A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”
It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.”
Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security.

articles.title: US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance
articles.body:
US Seizes $1.2 Billion In Crypto Stolen From Binance (cnbc.com) 13
			
		 	
				U.S. authorities have seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen during Binance's $6 billion October hack, which the FBI attributes to North Korean military-linked hackers known as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ also said it disrupted infrastructure behind the "FaceStealer" deepfake scam, blamed for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency. CNBC reports:  Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. [...] The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency." That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said. DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets. But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.
Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said. The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts -- sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

articles.title: FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
articles.body:
FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace 61
			
		 	
				The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports:  The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
[...] Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system's coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News. The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.

articles.title: Mississippi Picked Another Senator
articles.body:
While most of the results of last Tuesday’s elections are now official, some are still being finalized.1 It’s been less than 48 hours since Mississippi’s Senate race was finally called for Democrat Scott Colom. On the other hand, it’s been a couple weeks since I first saw his incredibly viral campaign ad.2
Friend-of-the-site Daniel J. pointed me to this interview with Ryan Sayles, the 27-year-old Mississippi content creator behind the ad.
You know, [I] just added the entertainment or funny pieces of it, like emphasizing the way he said the words and stuff like that. And then I shot it, edited it, and added the music to it.
I sat there and edited for like five hours. I’ve heard that man say “shit” a million times.
Me too, Ryan. Me too.3

- Alaska has decent reasons for taking so long in a tight race, as the Division of Elections explained: Alright, fine, fine. We can wait. ↩︎

articles.title: Elephants Found to Be Increasingly Isolated Leading to Fractured Social Networks
articles.body:
Elephants Found to be Increasingly Isolated, Leading to Fractured Social Networks
With a troubling decline in the population, researchers warn of a tipping point for the highly social animals
Published Date
Article Content
Key Takeaways
- UC San Diego researchers studied the social dynamics of hundreds of Asian elephants over more than a decade in Sri Lanka.
- They tracked a decrease in the population of the highly social animals that has led to fractured and more isolated communities.
- Surpassing a social “tipping point,” they warn, can be detrimental to the future of the animals.
Humans and many other social animals thrive in well-established community networks. Asian elephants are one example of a species that flourishes in groups that work together to access food and care for their young, among other social bonds.
University of California San Diego scientists in the School of Biological Sciences studying the intricacies of Asian elephant community structures have documented a troubling downturn in the population of the animals resulting in fractured social communities. Their study is published on the cover of the November 12 issue of Science.
Analyzing the social dynamics of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years at the Udawalawe National Park in Sri Lanka, the researchers studied key shifts in the demographics of the elephants that seemed to trigger social communities becoming smaller and more isolated.
“We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study, which was led by Postdoctoral Researcher Anastasia Madsen from the laboratory of Associate Professor Shermin de Silva in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution. de Silva also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.
The researchers’ analysis indicates a social structure tipping point. As the number of elephants in the population decreased over time, due to a combination of likely deaths, permanent emigrations of elephants and fewer incoming individuals, the population as a whole appears to have crossed a critical threshold that resulted in a shift from large, densely connected social communities, to smaller and less-connected social groupings.
“We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but new individuals are not coming into the population,” said Madsen. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.”
This new dynamic is a cause for concern, says Madsen, since the animals leverage their social groups and connections to forage, acquire information and raise young.
“We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” said de Silva. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.”
Many elephant populations are already impacted through deaths resulting from poaching and conflicts with humans. Other contributing factors may be disruptions in habitat connectivity and less food available for the elephants as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and surroundings.
The new social fracturing structure observed by the scientists may not be easily repaired, the researchers warn.
“In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” said Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.”
The new findings will serve future studies seeking to understand shifts in animal society structures, how to detect such tranformations and the factors responsible for vulnerabilities. The study also stimulates ongoing discussions for conserving elephant populations as humans expand into areas where elephants historically thrived.
“We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” said Madsen.
The researchers of the study were: Anastasia E. Madsen, T.V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva.
Funding for the research was provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Asian Elephant Conservation Grants (F11AP00258, F14AP00256 and F17AP00308); National Science Foundation (grant DBI-2305860); University of Pennsylvania; UC San Diego; and Trunks & Leaves Inc.

articles.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
articles.body:
Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident' (brickfanatics.com) 2
			
		 	
				LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident.
In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information.
The outage also dealt a significant blow to independent sellers who rely on BrickLink for income. Simon Webster, who operates stores on both BrickLink and rival marketplace Brick Owl, reported that his overall sales revenue fell 52% over a four-day period, even as sales through Brick Owl rose 79%. "Their comms are amateur at the best of times, but surely they should be able to send an email to let sellers and buyers alike know what is happening and what they're doing to rectify it," Webster said. "But no, we're all left in the dark."
The incident has renewed concerns about BrickLink's aging infrastructure. Founded in 2000 and acquired by LEGO in 2019, the marketplace reportedly runs on a complex collection of interconnected systems that makes modernization difficult. The Brick Fanatics report questions whether the 25-year-old platform remains fit for purpose and whether prolonged outages and security concerns could push sellers toward competing marketplaces like Brick Owl.

articles.title: Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI
articles.body:
Parents and Teachers Decry Google Pledge To Yank Search If Schools Block AI (theguardian.com) 52
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google's announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search. Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google's AI tools will also lose access to its search engine. [...] Parents and teachers across the country raised concerns to the Guardian about AI's potential to weaken students' critical-thinking skills and the growing influence of big tech in education. Some called on schools to consider alternative search engines, while others argued that students should be taught how to use AI responsibly rather than prevented from accessing it altogether.
Jen Atay, a 51-year-old teacher in Hawaii, lambasted Google's approach, saying: "When the software is free, you are the product, and it is inappropriate for Google to test or develop AI with minors. This should not be allowed at all." A 44-year-old father of two boys in Amissville, Virginia, said he worries that "AI will weaken people's ability to think critically. I use AI in my work, but it would not be effective if I did not have well over a decade of experience under my belt. Even the best models are often flat-out wrong in their responses." [...] Others questioned why schools should depend on Google at all.  An 84-year-old retiree and mother in Maryland, said: "Google decided to follow the evil path to riches. When they started, they were great. Today they are simply evil money grubbers  Schools should tell Google to go pound sand and simply have kids use DuckDuckGo or one of the other search engines  There is nothing Google offers that is not available from some other source." [...]
Not everyone believes blocking AI is the answer. Some argued that schools should focus on teaching students how to use the technology responsibly. A 67-year-old emerging technology teacher in Texas said: "I do not blame Google. AI is not going away. I've been very frustrated this year trying to teach AI literacy with AI blocked. Schools need to teach how to properly use AI, not block it." A California resident echoed that view, arguing that schools could use Google's AI tools to teach students to question the information they receive. "Google Search has existed since the 90s and it's crazy of them to completely remove it instead of just removing Gemini. That being said, I would like to see schools actually permit the use of Gemini and use it as an opportunity to show students how its sources aren't always valid and you can't trust everything an AI tells you," they said.

articles.title: Easy Homemade Cornbread
articles.body:
Cornbread is a highly underrated side dish. You can whip up this deliciously sweet and moist Homemade Cornbread recipe with just a few pantry staples, and it makes a perfect side dish for breakfast, lunch, or dinner! Serve it slathered with butter at breakfast, crumbled into your soup or chili at lunch, or as a side with your collard greens and pork chops for dinner. It’s inexpensive, comforting, and seriously easy to make, with 8 pieces costing just $1.27 ($0.16 each)! So toss that boxed mix and let me show you how it’s done for real. 😉
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
“Perfect cornbread! My cornbread always turned out too dry and crumbly – no more! Moist but still with the bit of crumbly and lightness cornbread should have. Really like cooking it in a pie dish and having wedges as well. Thank you!”
Rebecca
A Humble Side with Staying Power
I originally made this cornbread back in 2015 to help stretch a pot of stew further during one of my budget challenges, and it’s been a favorite ever since. I make it completely from scratch with yellow cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, milk, an egg, and cooking oil, most of which you’ve probably already got in your cupboard or fridge! It’s as simple as whisking the wet ingredients, combining them with the dry ingredients, and baking. I don’t even use a mixer and there’s no rising time to worry about, either.
But what I love most about this classic recipe is that it’s lightly sweetened, sitting somewhere between the sweeter, almost cake-like cornbread’s and the more savory Southern-style versions. Just ¼ cup of sugar adds a little sweetness while still letting that lovely corn flavor come through. I also use regular milk instead of buttermilk (so there’s no need to buy a whole carton that you might struggle to use up!).
It’s a simple everyday side, but I love serving a slice alongside a Thanksgiving or Christmas roast, too. You can even bake it the day before, which means one less thing to worry about when you’ve got a big holiday meal to prepare!
Recipe Success Tips
- Use baking powder, NOT baking soda! They’re not interchangeable. This recipe uses baking powder because it contains the ingredients needed to give the cornbread a tender crumb and good rise. Baking soda used in its place can leave an unpleasant, bitter taste and won’t give the same rise or result.
- Mix gently for tender cornbread. I know it’s tempting to keep stirring until everything is completely smooth, but you don’t want to do that here! Overmixing can develop the gluten in the flour and make the finished bread a little rubbery. Stir until everything is moistened. A few lumps are perfectly fine.
- Use the baking dish you’ve got. This amount of batter fits well into an 8×8 casserole dish, 9-inch pie plate, or a 10-inch cast iron skillet (although you should preheat the skillet as the oven preheats). Glass, ceramic, and cast iron work best, but you can also use metal baking dishes.
- Prefer savory over sweet? You can reduce the sugar to suit your tastes. Some readers have even left it out completely with good results, although changing the sugar can affect the browning and texture slightly.
- Make corn muffins instead! This is a great option if you want individual servings or something easy to grab and pack for lunch. Pour the batter into an oiled muffin tin, filling each well about ¾ full. Bake at the same temperature (425°F) for 16-18 minutes, or until the tops are golden brown. I usually get about 10 corn muffins from one batch (see photo).
Three Ways to Avoid Dry Cornbread
A little crumbliness is part of cornbread’s charm, but it shouldn’t fall apart the moment you slice it. Too much flour or cornmeal, or leaving it in the oven too long, can quickly turn a moist crumb dry. Here’s how I help keep this recipe tender without losing that classic cornmeal texture:
- The flour adds structure, and the oil keeps things tender. Cornmeal doesn’t form gluten, so I use equal cups of all-purpose flour and cornmeal to help the bread hold together. Then the oil helps keep the crumb soft, even after it cools, because unlike butter, it stays liquid at room temperature.
- Measure your flour and cornmeal carefully. Too much of either can throw off the balance of wet and dry ingredients, leaving you with a dry and crumbly bread. I recommend weighing them with a kitchen scale for the most consistent results (140 g flour and 150 g cornmeal).
- Don’t overbake! This recipe takes about 20 minutes at 425°F, but the exact time can vary depending on your baking dish. Look for golden-brown edges and a golden top, then insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs (see photo below). There’s no need to keep baking once it’s done, or you risk drying it out.
What to Serve with Cornbread
Cornbread is a great side dish for any thick and hearty soup, stew, or chili. I especially love serving it with a big bowl of my classic chili. I’ll usually either dip a warm slice into the sauce or crumble it straight into my bowl (my favorite way to use up day-old leftovers!). The mild sweetness works really well with smoky spices and a little heat. But really, you can serve this recipe in place of your usual dipping bread with any soup or stew you love. It’s also delicious layered into an easy cornbread salad with beans, corn, and veggies for a potluck or gathering (recipe coming soon!)
I also love a warm slice with a pat of butter melting right on top. Add a drizzle of honey (as much or as little as you like!), and you’ve got a delicious afternoon snack with a cup of coffee or a sweet side for your eggs and bacon at breakfast.
And don’t forget about the holidays! I’d happily swap the usual dinner rolls for a slice of cornbread alongside some roasted turkey breast, a batch of my homemade cranberry sauce, and all the Thanksgiving fixings. You can also take it a step further and use this recipe to make our cornbread dressing, which is loaded with savory herbs and vegetables and makes enough to feed a crowd!
How to Make Cornbread from Scratch step-by-step photos
Preheat the oven and prepare your baking dish: Gather and measure your ingredients, then preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C/200°C fan/Gas Mark 7). Grease a 9-inch pie plate, 10-inch cast iron skillet, or 8×8-inch baking dish with non-stick spray (or butter for a little extra flavor). I’ve always loved using my glass pie dish, but this time we used cast iron, and any of these options will work.
Combine the dry ingredients: In a large bowl, stir together 1 cup (150 g) yellow cornmeal, 1 cup (140 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 tsp (9 g) baking powder, and ½ tsp salt. Make sure everything is well mixed so the baking powder is evenly distributed throughout.
Whisk the wet ingredients: In a separate bowl, whisk together 1 cup (240 ml) milk, 1 large egg, and ¼ cup (60 ml) cooking oil until the egg is fully broken up and everything is well combined.
Gently mix the batter: Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir just until everything is moistened and there are no dry pockets of flour. Don’t keep stirring until the batter is completely smooth. A few lumps are perfectly fine, and overmixing can make the finished bread a little rubbery.
Bake until golden brown: Pour the batter into your prepared dish and spread it evenly. Bake for about 20 minutes, or until the top and edges are golden brown.
The top may crack a little, and that’s perfectly normal! To check it’s done, insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cut into 8 pieces and serve. Enjoy!
More Cornbread Recipes to Try
- Give the classic recipe a cheesy, slightly spicy twist with my Chili Cheese Cornbread, made with cheddar, chili powder, and sweet corn kernels.
- I love combining two comfort food favorites in my Chili Cornbread Skillet. The homemade cornbread bakes right on top of a hearty bean chili, with a layer of melted cheddar in between!
- Mashed sweet potato, sour cream, cinnamon, and nutmeg make this Sweet Potato Cornbread extra moist, rich, and full of warm fall flavors.
Other Easy Classic Bread Recipes
Our Easy Homemade Cornbread recipe was originally published 9/5/15. It was retested, reworked, and republished to be better than ever 11/13/26.

articles.title: Crustless Quiche
articles.body:
Crustless Quiche
This crustless quiche recipe offers the tender texture that you love in a regular quiche. It's an easy, healthy, high-protein egg dish!
Posted by Kathryne Taylor on November 13, 2026
Craving quiche, but don’t want to fuss with a crust? This eggy wonder is perfectly tender inside, like a regular quiche! You’d never guess it, but there’s cottage cheese inside, which makes it nice and soft, similar to egg bites. This protein-rich quiche recipe is the perfect way to balance morning muffins and breads.
If you’re particular about your eggs like I am, you’ll appreciate this recipe. It’s made differently from a baked frittata. While I love a well-made frittata (you can find all my tips here), this recipe is a safer bet. Even if you cook it a couple of minutes too long, it won’t turn brown on the bottom or spongy like a frittata can. Try it, and you’ll see!
How to Make a Quiche Without Crust
You’ll find the full recipe at the bottom of the post, but here’s why this recipe works so well.
1. Cottage cheese instead of milk or cream.
It’s the secret ingredient that offers a very subtle tang and extra protein. Once blended, the lumpy texture disappears, which explains why I’d never guess it was there. Quiche typically has a high milk-to-eggs ratio, and the cottage cheese helps the eggs firm up just right without spending a long time in the oven.
2. Baked in a water bath.
I promise, the water bath is easy to manage, and it makes all the difference. We’ll bake the egg dish on a rimmed baking sheet filled with a small amount of hot water. The steam from the water bath gives these bites a luscious, smooth texture by gently cooking the eggs, preventing them from rising so quickly that they develop big air bubbles. Without the water bath, the eggs would be firmer and brown at the bottom.
Watch how to make this recipe
Flavor Variations that Work
The ingredients shown here are inspired by traditional French quiche Florentine, which typically includes sautéed spinach with onion and Gruyère or Swiss cheese. You can’t go wrong with this classic combination. That said, you can easily change up the greens, onion and cheese:
- Instead of spinach, you could sauté chopped kale, chard or collard greens until tender (remove the tough ribs before cooking).
- Instead of yellow onion, you could use 1/4 cup chopped green onion.
- As for the cheese, anything goes. Cheddar, Parmesan or goat cheese would be lovely.
You can also add up to 1 cup tender or cooked vegetables, cut into bite-sized pieces. Try cooking bell pepper with your onions, or adding quartered cherry tomatoes.
Cheese Tip
Buy your own block of cheese and grate it before using. Pre-shredded and pre-crumbled cheeses are coated in cellulose powder, so they don’t melt as nicely.
Quiche Serving Suggestions
This easy, protein-rich quiche makes a great breakfast or brunch, but you could also make it for lunch or dinner. Here are my suggestions to build a full meal.
- For a simple occasion, round out your meal with crusty sourdough (toasted if you’d like) and a little green salad.
- For a full-blown spread, consider serving quiche with crispy hash browns or any of my pancake recipes, which you can cook on the stove while the quiche bakes in the oven. Or instead of pancakes, make muffins the day before.
- For a fun summer salad, try my Easy Tomato Salad or Summertime Fruit Salad. In the cooler months, try my French Carrot Salad or Favorite Green Salad with Apples, Cranberries and Pepitas.
Please let me know how your quiche turns out in the comments. I love hearing from you.
Crustless Quiche
This crustless quiche recipe offers the tender texture that you love in a regular quiche. It’s an easy, healthy, high-protein egg dish! This spinach, onion and cheese version was inspired by traditional quiche Florentine. Check the post for variations. Recipe yields 6 medium slices; you could likely bake two quiches in the oven at once.
Ingredients
- 8 large eggs
- 1 cup (8 ounces) cottage cheese (4% milkfat or higher, made with whole milk)
- ¼ teaspoon fine salt
- 10 twists of freshly ground black pepper
- 2 teaspoons unsalted butter, plus more for greasing the pan
- ½ cup chopped yellow onion
- 2 cups (3.5 ounces) finely chopped spinach
- 1 packed cup (4 ounces) freshly grated Gruyère or Swiss cheese
Instructions
- Preheat the oven to 325 degrees Fahrenheit, and grease a glass pie plate with butter. In a kettle or medium saucepan, bring 3 cups of water to a boil and maintain a simmer until it’s needed.
- In a blender, combine the eggs, cottage cheese, and the salt and pepper. Blend on high for 8 to 10 seconds, just until the mixture is smooth and frothy (no longer!). Set it aside.
- Melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and a pinch of salt, and stir to combine. Cook until the onion is tender and translucent, about 3 to 5 minutes. Add the spinach, and cook until the spinach is wilted and reduced in volume, about 1 to 2 minutes. Remove the mixture from the heat and let it cool for a couple of minutes, then stir it into the blender mixture. Stir in half of the cheese.
- Place the prepared pie plate on a large, rimmed baking sheet. Carefully pour the egg mixture into the pie plate. Sprinkle the remaining cheese on top, then transfer the stacked pans to the oven. Carefully pour the hot water into the sheet pan, enough to submerge the bottom of the pie pan by at least ⅛ inch.
- Bake for 34 to 39 minutes, until the eggs are puffed and appear cooked, and the center of the quiche jiggles just a bit when you give it a gentle shimmy.
- Remove the pie plate from the sheet pan of water in the oven, and let it cool for at least 10 minutes on a cooling rack before serving. Leftover quiche will keep in the fridge, covered, for up to 4 days, or in the freezer for up to 3 months. Reheat slices in a microwave or on a rimmed baking sheet in a 300-degree oven until warmed through (they will release some moisture while reheating, which you can discard).
Nutrition
The information shown is an estimate provided by an online nutrition calculator. It should not be considered a substitute for a professional nutritionist’s advice. See our full nutrition disclosure here.

articles.title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
articles.body:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years.
Intel, Microsoft, and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from the company’s leadership crisis.
As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel.
“Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch.
Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen.
The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.”
Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis, Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list.
Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away.
According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.”
Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips.
Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.”
And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s.
“These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said.

articles.title: Hawaii DOT: All West Coast flights halted by SpaceX debris after FAA ground stop
articles.body:
FAA lifts nationwide ground stop: What Hawaii travelers should know
Travelers should continue checking with their carriers.
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - A nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that disrupted several domestic flights to and from Hawaiʻi was lifted at around 3:20 p.m. Friday.
The Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation said in an update that both the nationwide ground stop and a temporary pause for space debris had been lifted.
Delays may continue as airlines accommodate passengers from earlier flights, officials said.
RELATED POST: Flights halted at airports across US due to air traffic control communications problems, FAA says
Initial ground stop affected domestic travel
The FAA issued the ground stop following a communications issue affecting air traffic control centers. Flight disruptions had been intermittent with restrictions changing throughout the day.
Hawaiʻi Department of Transportation Director Ed Sniffen said officials were notified of the ground stop at about 10:50 a.m. for domestic flights to and from the continental U.S.
Interisland flights were not affected, he said.
“There’s been adjustments throughout. Initially, flights, international flights were unrestricted. Then we got notifications that there are some conflicts with the international flights,” Sniffen said.
At around 12:30 p.m., Sniffen said some flights had been cleared to leave Hawaiʻi for the West Coast.
Officials were repositioning aircraft and planning to use taxiways and some runways for parking to make room for arriving planes, he said.
SpaceX debris halted flights again
In a 1:55 p.m. update, the DOT announced all West Coast flights had been halted due to debris from a SpaceX launch.
SpaceX launched its Starship rocket from Texas on Friday, but its first-stage booster malfunctioned and ended up in the Gulf after an automatic abort, according to The Associated Press. The spacecraft continued toward orbit.
“The big message to all the public is things are changing pretty quickly,” Sniffen said. “Before you come down to the airport, make sure you reach out to your carrier.”
11/13/26 1:55PM: All west coast flights have been halted due to debris from SpaceX launch. Please continue to check with your carrier for further updates. https://t.co/Et1gtFbfe7
— Hawaii DOT (@DOTHawaii) November 13, 2026
What travelers should know
Hawaiian and Alaska airlines said a flexible travel policy was in place for guests who need to change their plans.
The airlines said it would take time to safely return operations to schedule after the ground stop was lifted.
Nationwide ground stops are rare. A pilot notification system outage prompted one in January 2023; the previous nationwide stop followed the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

articles.title: Anthropic Upgrades Claude Code Projects to Run Parallel AI Workers Hands-Free
articles.body:
Anthropic Upgrades Claude Code Projects to Run Parallel AI Workers Hands-Free
Anthropic ships a proactive coordinator, shareable read-only threads, reminders, and /btw and /fork slash commands to Claude Code Projects.
- Claude Code Projects coordinator is now proactive, answering questions and pushing thread status updates in chat.
- Individual threads can be shared as read-only links to signed-in Claude users; threads with local computer access are excluded.
- Reminders let a thread hide itself and resurface in the project chat at a scheduled time.
- /btw opens a side thread for tangents; /fork branches a new thread from the current one.
- Threads panel adds a recents row and artifact thumbnails for easier retrieval across large projects.
- Public beta on Pro and Max across web, desktop, and the latest mobile app; Team and Enterprise excluded.
Anthropic has updated Claude Code Projects with proactive coordinator messages, read-only thread sharing, reminders, branching commands, and improved artifact navigation. The changes reduce the monitoring required when several cloud sessions work in parallel.
Each project is a long-running conversation with a coordinator that assigns work to threads. Every thread runs as an independent Claude Code cloud session with its own repository copy and Git branch. The coordinator directs the project from thread reports, while overlapping code changes surface as standard Git merge conflicts when branches are combined.
The coordinator reports without prompting
The coordinator now answers questions directly in project chat and posts status updates as threads progress. Previously, developers had to monitor the thread list to find sessions waiting for input. The updated behavior brings pending decisions, completed tasks, and blocked work into the main conversation.
Read-only links stop at local access
Individual threads can now be shared through read-only links with anyone signed in to Claude. A developer can open the thread menu, select Share, and send the generated URL without exposing the rest of the project.
Threads that accessed a local computer remain unshareable. The restriction prevents shared transcripts from exposing local file contents, shell output, or other machine data gathered during the session.
Park a thread or branch the work
The two slash commands were already available in regular Claude Code sessions. Their addition to Projects brings the same branching workflow to coordinated, multi-thread work.
Artifacts surface sooner
The threads panel now places recently opened, updated, and pinned threads in a row at the top. Each thread can also display thumbnails for generated documents, diagrams, and other artifacts, with the previews controlled through view settings.
The redesign simplifies project settings and local-folder access as well. Anthropic has released the changes on the web, desktop clients, and the latest mobile app.
Parallelism draws from the same allowance
Anthropic introduced the public beta on September 17 for Pro and Max subscribers who joined the waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans remain unsupported. Eligible subscribers who lack access can still join the waitlist.
Projects carry no separate fee, but every worker consumes the subscriber’s existing Claude Code allowance. Anthropic limits accounts to 200 new threads per day across all projects. A thread that reaches a usage limit pauses and resumes automatically when capacity becomes available.
Project usage appears separately in the usage controls, and developers can choose the model and effort level for the coordinator and worker threads. New projects default to Opus for both roles, with low effort for the coordinator and high effort for workers. Several high-effort sessions running at once can exhaust plan limits faster than a single Claude Code session.
Where many threads pay off
Projects fit engineering work that can be divided into independent tasks and reconciled through branches and pull requests. Anthropic’s examples include:
- Performance work: Assign separate threads to profile endpoints, test optimizations, and open pull requests. A target such as p75 checkout latency refers to the response time at or below which 75% of requests finish.
- Cross-repository migrations: Connect API, web, and mobile repositories, then create one thread per codebase and report the required merge order.
- Batch changes: Distribute refactors, dependency upgrades, test repairs, or bug-triage items across parallel sessions.
Tasks with strict dependencies still require developers to sequence pull requests and resolve conflicts. Projects also remain cloud-only and limited to Claude Code, while parallel workers draw from the same plan limits. Small changes that fit one branch and one context window generally consume fewer resources in a regular Claude Code session.

articles.title: Unsloth Qwen3.8-27B Quantizations – Dynamic v3.1 Update
articles.body:
Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally
Guide to running Qwen3.8 quants including Qwen3.8-27B on your local setup.
Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop.
Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models.
Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include:
- Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex
- MTP enabled for fast inference
- Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more
Unsloth quants: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF
Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026)
We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat.
Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better!
We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1, and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. We used 256K context lengths for all agentic benchmarks, and 128K for the rest. We followed the same methodology for Qwen3.8-27B as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next which also utilized our V3.1 preview algorithm.

💡 Thinking + Preserve Thinking
Qwen3.8 has Preserve Thinking which leaves the thinking trace from the previous conversation. This increases the number of tokens you use, but could increase accuracy in continued conversations. Unsloth has 'Think' and Preserved Thinking toggles for Qwen3.8 (see right):

- medium: balancing accuracy and speed

- none
Run Qwen3.8 Guide
You can now run Qwen3.8-27B in llama.cpp and Unsloth Desktop. Feel free to change quantization type.
- Hugging Face: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF • Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
- ModelScope: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF • Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
🦥 Run Qwen3.8 in Unsloth Desktop
Qwen3.8 can run in Unsloth Desktop, an open-source UI app for local AI. Unsloth automatically offloads to RAM and detects multiGPU setups. With Unsloth Desktop, you can run models locally on MacOS, Windows, Linux and:
- Search, download, run GGUFs, MLX and safetensor models
- Self-healing tool calling + web search
- Code execution (Python, Bash)
- Automatic inference parameter tuning (temp, top-p, etc.)
- Fast CPU + GPU inference via MLX and llama.cpp
- Train LLMs 2x faster with 70% less VRAM

Go to Unsloth Chat or Model hub and search for Qwen3.8 in the search bar and download your desired model and quant.
