articles.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
articles.body:
Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.
I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.
Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels
people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice
for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a
terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about
this.
The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:
So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.
Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.
Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:
Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.
What I'd use it for
- Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
- Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
- Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
- Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
- Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.
Up close
The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:
The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:
Charts
Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:
And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:
In motion
Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:
Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:
What box characters can't do
The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.
Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.
You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.
Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's
pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box
(pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never
get copied, which cuts both ways.
How it works
A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.
The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters (▖▗▘▝ and
friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a
neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better
way to do that part. One problem at a time.
The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.
Styles and joints
Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.
When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The
stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below.
That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its
neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the
focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.
The wire format
Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \
The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \     bottom edge, blue: an underline
hello
ESC [ 0 m                                              SGR 0 clears the pen
There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching
the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives
without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box
characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it,
the same as any unknown DCS.
The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.
Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.
The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b). That's v1 in the old sense, before
we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write
down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.
Prior art
Parts of this have been done before:
- DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.
- SGR 51 to 65: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.
- The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses
and X/Open curses (WA_TOP, WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the
closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
- IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields.
What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.
My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.
The awkward (edge) cases
When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.
Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.
Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.
Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.
On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.
Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.
Try it
The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git
cd ghostty
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native
open zig-out/Ghostty.app
Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py            # the default view
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles   # line styles, joints and outside fill
Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j
junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off
so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag (--placement, --styles
and so on) if you want to start on it.
The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git
cd ratatui
cargo run -p tiling-panes
Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click
opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade
alternate cells and see where the edges are.
The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:
To run it:
cargo run -p cell-border-top
It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a
better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the
boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys.
It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency.
What I'd like to hear
I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.
Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.
Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.
On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.
Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.
Try it
The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git
cd ghostty
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native
open zig-out/Ghostty.app
Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py            # the default view
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles   # line styles, joints and outside fill
Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j
junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off
so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag (--placement, --styles
and so on) if you want to start on it.
The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git
cd ratatui
cargo run -p tiling-panes
Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click
opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade
alternate cells and see where the edges are.
The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:
To run it:
cargo run -p cell-border-top
It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a
better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the
boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys.
It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency.
What I'd like to hear
I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

articles.title: No AI Slop: A Manifesto
articles.body:
No AI Slop: A Manifesto
Written by the speakers and attendees of AIE Code Summit 2026
In 2001, 17 software engineers and leaders got together at a ski lodge in Snowbird, Utah to understand the biggest challenge of their time: heavyweight, documentation-driven software development processes.
Out of this we got the Agile Manifesto, four values and twelve principles that changed how most of the industry builds software.
Today we convene to build our own manifesto - the No AI Slop manifesto.
AI increasingly helps us write our code, docs, plans, and messages. We've all been on the receiving end of slop, and most of us have sent some too. Through this work, we have come to value:
Outcomes over output
Understanding over speed
Our own thinking over a model's first draft
Better work over easier work
Improving the system over patching the output
The world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.
We believe:
- AI is the most useful tool most of us have ever worked with, but a swarm of agents can produce more work in a single day than a person can review in our lifetime.
- Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.
- Using AI doesn't necessarily make something slop. Slop happens when we pass AI output along without taking responsibility for the quality or the reader's experience.
- AI cannot replace human judgement, it can only amplify our judgement (or lack thereof).
- Slop is asymmetric. The cost of producing a thousand-line PR or a ten-page doc is approaching zero, while the cost of reviewing it remains constant.
- In code, even before AI, slop proliferates when we repeatedly work around problems instead of solving them correctly. It comes from tools that lean HEAVILY toward adding rather than subtracting.
- A lot of slop comes from pressure. Companies are pushing their people to redefine what is humanly possible.
- Slop compounds. The more slop sits in our knowledge base, in chat, in code, the more of it the next agent reads and copies.
- The more slop flying around a team, the more we lose the will to fight it. Communication and quality get worse over time, not better.
Thus we the undersigned resolve that:
- Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.
- We fight slop because AI should make our work better, not just easier.
- We optimize systems, tools, and products for efficient elicitation of human intent and for efficient human understanding.
- We do our own thinking when working with a model. We explore resources, code, and prior art to truly understand the problem before the work starts.
- We own the intent, taste, and consequences of what we ship, however much AI helps us make it.
- When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.
- When someone sends us slop, we tell them, kindly, and ask them to review it first. Most of us have needed that same note at some point.
- There will always be alpha in reviewing something. As models improve, we may stop reading most of the code. We may still review a plan, design, or result, because if we don't, we just get the same output as everyone else.
- Agent reviews, linters, and verifiers are useful but not sufficent. For now, we still review at least some subset of the outputs. What subset depends on the stakes.
- What shipped, who's using it, and how it's helping them matters FAR MORE than lines of code, prs merged, tokens spent, or the number of agents running in parallel.
- Unreviewed output isn't always necessarily bad. One-shot prompts and vibe coding are high leverage tools. "Slop" is bad when it undermines our outcome -- a useful product, a maintainable system, or saving ourselves and our teammates time and energy.
- When a mistake shows up twice, we scale ourselves and our team by improving the system and its guardrails. Anything a linter, type checker, or automated check can catch, we let it catch.
And finally:
- None of us has this figured out. We're each relearning what we will and won't accept, and there's no single right answer.
Again, the world moves especially fast these days, but the goal of these resolutions is to embrace our important human role in harnessing AI safely, responsibly, in a way that creates value for everyone, and that will be relevant for years to come.
We look forward to working with the community to evolve these beliefs as the world changes. Comments and feedback on this document are welcome. What is slop? Why does slop happen? Why is slop worth fighting? How do we fight slop?
Special thanks to Philip Kiely, Swyx, Lucas Meijer, Rebecca Bakels, Tejas Kumar, Natalie Serrino, Francisco Javier Arceo, Kent C. Dodds, Ankit Jain, Brandon Waselnuk, Mihail Eric, Justin McCarthy, Raz Berman Gold, Yacine Mahdid, Justin Poehnelt, Lauren Tan, and Kyle Mistele for contributions to this project.
More resources
- No More Slop - swyx declares war on slop, AIE Code Summit, November 2025
- Please stop the slop - Tejas Kumar on how he keeps slop out of his own writing
- Vibe Coding Our Way to Disaster - Jake Nations on why the thinking can't be handed to AI, only made bigger by it
- Ghostty AI Usage Policy - Ghostty Maintainers on the importance of human understanding and care
- Why Software Factories Fail - Dex begs us to please keep reading at least some of the code
Sign the manifesto
Sign the manifesto
Add a gist comment with any or all of: name, company, X handle, LinkedIn, and we'll regularly pull signatures into the manifesto.
Signed-off by: [any of: name, company, x, linkedin, etc]

articles.title: Someone's Impersonating This Blog
articles.body:
I was googling the name of my website, as one does occasionally, and was surprised to see a link to one of my blog posts on mataroa.site. At first I figured it was just an alternate domain name for mataroa.blog, but no, when you type mataroa.site into your browser, it shows you my blog. It's the only thing that's hosted there.
My next thought was that someone bought me a URL, but that can't be the case either: using a custom domain on mataroa requires a premium account, which I don't have. For anything but a plain redirect, I would have needed to set up the A record my end.
I then realized that the version of my blog on that site doesn't have the latest post. The most recent update on the homepage is my Aug 21 entry. When you scroll down and start clicking some of the older links, you get 404 pages. You also get a 404 if you try to post a comment, load the RSS feed or view standalone pages like the AI statement.
Someone scraped my blog and created a website to impersonate me. They're also impersonating mataroa, since using the name implies some sort of official connection.
They're re-hosting the stolen images on their own server, and they all have a watermark. Bizarrely, the watermark is mattbee.mataroa.blog, my real URL. I assume this is to somehow make it seem legitimate, like it's an officially-sanctioned mirror, but I don't know who they think is going to care. It's not like they're stealing from a site with name recognition.
When you view the source of a blog post, it's identical to the rendered HTML except that there are two Cloudflare scripts at the bottom, one to obfuscate the mailto: link in the footer (which doesn't work1) and one for analytics.
When you view the source of the index, there's a hidden link at the bottom to a Chinese github.io page for a website cloning tool.
I have no idea why I was targeted for impersonation. It should be obvious this isn't a high-value website.2 It's a personal blog where I write what's relevant to me, and that rarely overlaps with anything other people care about. If the subject matter didn't tip them off, it should be clear from the 0 comments on most posts that this is not an enterprise ripe for monetization.
If they just wanted a fake blog to scam adsense, surely a large language model would happily spew out more SEO-friendly slop than anything I have to offer. If their goal was to leech off the popularity of mataroa, why not impersonate one of the blogs with multiple front-page appearances on the orange website? Surely they have more SEO juice than me. Nothing about this makes any sense.
Anyway, the URL is registered with Namecheap, so I sent them an abuse report. I have no idea if they'll act on it. They don't seem to have a good track record of giving a shit unless the content is actually hosted with them.
It's hosted with Cloudflare, and the abuse reporting form they insist you use straight-up doesn't work. Click "Submit an abuse report" and it'll take you to a completely blank page. Very encouraging.
I'd have to dox myself to do a DMCA takedown, and I don't have the legal resources to do anything when it gets ignored. So if neither evil corporation cares to do anything, I guess I can just get fucked. I figure the best thing I can do to protect myself is document everything here. If you see a link to mataroa.site, it's not affiliated with me or mataroa. It seems like it isn't set up to scam people or distribute malware at the moment, but it probably will in the future. Be careful.
Edit
The index page also has a meta tag with a verification code for mitgo.com, a fake-looking website with some word salad identifying it as some kind of ad/SEO scamming platform or service. Will try to investigate this further.

articles.title: Comparing Jensen to Steve Jobs Is Stupid
articles.body:
Comparing Jensen to Steve Jobs is Stupid
Time for a history lesson.
Many are criticizing Nvidia for kicking out Jensen, saying it is akin to Apple "firing" Steve Jobs in 1985. While the comparison is wrong—Jobs was pushed out for much less nefarious reasons—it also implies that Apple would have succeeded earlier instead of waiting for Jobs' return in 1997.
This misses the entire redemption arc Jobs goes through at NeXT Computer. He leaves Apple and takes his pride and poor management skills with him. In time, all of his NeXT co-founders leave, repelled by Steve's toxicity. He burns an absurd amount of money on hard-headed decisions, while building a beautiful workstation that ultimately few buy.
When NeXT goes nearly bankrupt and lays off a mass portion of the company, Jobs is publicly humiliated—rightly so, because there was no one else to blame. NeXT was intentionally a one-man show.
It's in NeXT's software pivot that Jobs begins to redeem himself. He becomes a stronger collaborator, working more harmoniously with his teams as they humbly keep the company alive. It eventually leads them to the Apple acquisition, and Jobs returns as a completely different person than when he was oustered.
I highly recommend Geoffrey Cain's book, Steve Jobs in Exile, which is a vivid account of this forgotten episode. NeXT is everything for Steve Jobs—there would most likely be no Apple today without his fall from grace.

articles.title: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem
articles.body:
Hi all,
the technical leadership committee of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped!
We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational.
We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives.
We tried to keep the community proposal process as light as possible. However, we believe that fairness and participation are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback.
Below is our vision. Feel free to get in touch with us!
The TLC’s shared vision
We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation:
- It is good for humans to write by hand: Type safety, powerful abstractions and referential transparency have enabled engineers all over the world in startups and big tech to deliver and maintain complex systems.
- It is good for responsible AI workflows: review is a significant bottleneck in modern AI-workflows and Haskell’s strengths heavily favor the reviewer. Additionally, the ability to quickly design eDSLs and express constraints where it matters allows to set up strong guardrails for code generation, without losing flexibility.
There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly.
We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone:
- Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability
- Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity
- Industry: focussing on stability and scaling
A vision of productivity
Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance!
Iteration speed
Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows.
While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2.
Debugging and profiling
Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries:
- live step-through debugging
- actually useful stack traces
- beautiful performance analysis reports
And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP).
Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase.
Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools.
Onboarding and DevX
In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole.
- installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked
- documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck
- tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support
This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as:
- write programs that do one thing and do it well
- write programs that work together
- write programs that are extensible
Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans.
A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem
Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost.
To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to:
- have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems
- have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly
- make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations
- build a robust cryptography library stack
- harden our supply chain
We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell.
A vision of stability
What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes?
While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway.
The questions we need to answer along the way are:
- how can users opt out of breaking changes?
- how long can we keep support windows open?
- how can we make the upgrade experience better?
Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn.
We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem.
A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem
All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other.
We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world.
We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values.

We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone:
- Beginners: the onboarding experience must be our benchmark for usability
- Experts: enabling advanced workflows and improving productivity
- Industry: focussing on stability and scaling
A vision of productivity
Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance!
Iteration speed
Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows.
While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2.
Debugging and profiling
Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries:
- live step-through debugging
- actually useful stack traces
- beautiful performance analysis reports
And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP).
Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase.
Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools.
Onboarding and DevX
In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole.
- installation so quick that you’re wondering whether the installer even worked
- documentation so comprehensive and accessible that you never get stuck
- tooling so intuitive that you don’t have to constantly ask for support
This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as:
- write programs that do one thing and do it well
- write programs that work together
- write programs that are extensible
Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans.
A vision of a secure and trustworthy ecosystem
Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost.
To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to:
- have the fastest incident response time among language ecosystems
- have penetration testers go through our infrastructure regularly
- make end users aware of vulnerabilities and mitigations
- build a robust cryptography library stack
- harden our supply chain
We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell.
A vision of stability
What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes?
While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway.
The questions we need to answer along the way are:
- how can users opt out of breaking changes?
- how long can we keep support windows open?
- how can we make the upgrade experience better?
Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn.
We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem.
A vision of a flourishing open source ecosystem
All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other.
We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world.
We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values.

articles.title: Lonewolf 0.3 – A standalone XMPP server written in Rust
articles.body:
Repository navigation
The big one in this release is federation: Lonewolf can now talk to other XMPP servers. We also added direct TLS and a handful of extensions that desktop clients rely on.
Lonewolf is still pre-1.0 and runs as a single node. Full XMPP compliance and clustering are on the roadmap.
What's new
Federation
Your users can now exchange messages, presence, IQs, and roster subscriptions with people on other XMPP servers. If a host has a certificate and a public DNS name, federation is on by default, with nothing extra to configure.
Lonewolf authenticates peers by certificate only. The other server needs a trusted certificate and SASL EXTERNAL support. We don't support Server Dialback.
When the other server supports it, both directions share a single connection (XEP-0288). Servers also tell each other their stanza size and idle limits up front (XEP-0478).
Federation checks certificate revocation lists published by the CA, fetched over plain HTTP. If a CRL can't be downloaded, the connection goes ahead anyway. You can turn downloads off with s2s.tls.fetch_crls = false, or point s2s.tls.crls_path at a local file to use only that.
Direct TLS
Clients and servers can now connect with TLS from the first byte (XEP-0368), using new dedicated listeners. Outbound federation discovers both STARTTLS and direct TLS endpoints.
More for desktop clients
- Private XML Storage (XEP-0049) gives clients a place to keep private settings and legacy bookmarks.
- Software Version (XEP-0092) answers "what server is this?" queries. It doesn't reveal the operating system unless you turn that on.
Both are enabled by default.
Short-lived certificates
Use letsencrypt.certificate_profile to pick one of the profiles your CA advertises, including short-lived certificates. If you change the profile, Lonewolf renews early so the new one takes effect right away.
SCRAM-SHA-512 (opt-in)
You can now enable SCRAM-SHA-512 and SCRAM-SHA-512-PLUS. Be aware that they come from an expired Internet-Draft, not an RFC, and aren't registered with IANA.
Even if you leave SHA-512 login disabled, new accounts and password changes now store credentials that v0.2.0 can't read, so rolling back isn't straightforward.
See the standards reference for exactly what's supported and the configuration reference for every setting and its default.
Build from source
Grab Source code (tar.gz) or Source code (zip) below, extract it, and run:
cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl -p lonewolfbench
The benchmark tool is now called lonewolfbench instead of lonewolf-bench, so update any scripts that call it. All you need is a stable Rust toolchain and a system linker on Linux or macOS. The quick start walks you through setup.
Full changelog: v0.2.0…v0.3.0
Licensed under Apache-2.0.

articles.title: Show HN: Reflota – Open-source data recovery for NTFS/FAT disks with phased copy
articles.body:
Recuperá archivos de discos, pendrives y tarjetas (NTFS, FAT32, FAT16, FAT12 y exFAT), incluso los que borraste. Gratis, de código abierto y en modo solo lectura.
Cuando Windows dice "el disco no está formateado", una carpeta no abre o el explorador se cuelga, muchas veces los archivos siguen ahí. Reflota los reconstruye leyendo el disco directamente: en NTFS lee toda la tabla maestra (MFT) y arma el árbol de carpetas con la información que cada archivo guarda de su propia carpeta; en FAT y exFAT lee las carpetas y sigue las cadenas de clusters.
También encuentra archivos borrados y te dice cuántos de ellos siguen recuperables. Y si el disco se formateó o ya no tiene nombres, puede buscar archivos por su contenido, encontrar particiones perdidas y hacer una copia segura de un disco que está fallando.
Estado: beta. Funciona, pero cada disco dañado es distinto. Probalo primero con una copia de lo importante si podés.
Novedades todavía sin probar en discos reales (se verificaron con imágenes de prueba, no con hardware): FAT16/FAT12, búsqueda de RAW de cámara/PSD/RAR, reconstrucción de JPEG fragmentados, buscador por nombre y copia por fases. Si probás alguna con un disco real, contá cómo te fue en Issues.
Bajá Reflota.exe desde la sección Releases. No necesita instalación ni Python.
Como el programa no está firmado digitalmente, Windows puede mostrar "Windows protegió su PC": tocá Más información → Ejecutar de todas formas. Algunos antivirus desconfían de los programas que leen discos de forma directa; el código es abierto y podés compilar el .exe vos mismo (ver más abajo). Junto a cada Release se publica el hash SHA256 para comprobar que la descarga no se corrompió.
- Abrí Reflota. Aparece la lista de tus discos y unidades.
- Tildá lo que querés recuperar, todo en el mismo árbol:
  - Tildar un disco o una partición → se copia todo.
  - Entrá en la partición y tildá solo carpetas o archivos → se copia solo eso.
  - El tamaño total se calcula solo mientras tildás.
  - Activá Incluir archivos borrados para ver también lo que se borró: aparece en rojo, en su carpeta original, con su estado.
  - Buscar por nombre (arriba del árbol): escribí parte del nombre (factura), un patrón (*.pdf, foto_??.jpg) y apretá Enter. Busca sin importar mayúsculas ni acentos, en la partición elegida (o en todas las que ya abriste), incluye lo borrado y muestra los resultados como un grupo nuevo del árbol que se tilda igual que lo demás. Primero abrí la partición (clic en su flecha).
- Abajo, elegí la carpeta donde copiar (en otro disco) y apretá RECUPERAR.
Podés parar cuando quieras y volver a empezar: lo que ya se copió no se repite.
Windows no deja leer un disco "en crudo" sin permisos de administrador (le pasa a cualquier programa de recuperación). Reflota abre sin pedirlos y los pide recién cuando tocás un disco para leerlo; ahí se reabre con el aviso de Windows. El programa nunca escribe en el disco de origen.
Elegí primero un disco o una partición en la lista.
Buscar archivos por contenido. Reconoce los archivos por su forma interna, sin necesitar nombres ni carpetas. Sirve cuando el disco se formateó, la tabla de archivos está destruida o el archivo borrado ya perdió su nombre. Podés buscar solo en el espacio libre (rápido, ideal para lo borrado) o en todo el disco o la partición. Los resultados aparecen en el mismo árbol, agrupados por tipo, y se recuperan igual que lo demás (tildar y RECUPERAR). Detecta: fotos (JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, WebP, HEIC, TIFF), fotos RAW de cámara (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RW2, PEF, RAF), PSD/PSB de Photoshop, videos (MP4/MOV/3GP, AVI, MKV/WebM), audio (MP3, M4A, WAV), documentos (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, ODT/ODS/ODP, DOC/XLS/PPT, EPUB), comprimidos (ZIP, RAR, 7Z, JAR, APK) y bases de datos SQLite. El largo exacto de cada archivo se calcula leyendo su estructura (no se corta "a ojo"), y los archivos que contienen otros archivos adentro (como una miniatura en una foto) salen enteros. Los nombres originales no se pueden recuperar: salen numerados (recuperado_00012.jpg). Los archivos que estaban fragmentados (partidos en pedazos no contiguos) normalmente no se pueden rearmar y pueden salir incompletos o mezclados, salvo las fotos JPEG si tildás Reconstruir fotos JPEG fragmentadas: Reflota decodifica la foto hasta donde deja de ser válida y busca el pedazo que la continúa; solo la entrega si el resultado cierra exacto (todos los bloques de imagen y el final del archivo). Es mucho más lento, funciona con JPEG «baseline» (los de cámaras y celulares; no los progresivos) y puede no lograrlo cuando hay muchos fragmentos o el hueco está lleno de otras fotos parecidas: en ese caso la foto simplemente no aparece (no entrega una foto equivocada a propósito, pero conviene mirar el resultado).
Buscar particiones perdidas. Recorre el disco entero buscando los inicios de particiones NTFS, FAT32, FAT16/12 y exFAT, aunque la tabla de particiones esté borrada y hasta con los sectores de arranque destruidos (usa sus copias de respaldo). Las que encuentra se agregan a la lista. Puede tardar bastante en discos grandes y se puede parar.
Crear imagen del disco (copia segura). Cuando un disco falla, lo mejor es copiarlo una sola vez a un archivo y trabajar sobre esa copia, sin seguir forzando el original. La copia va por fases, como hacen las herramientas de rescate profesionales: primero lee rápido todo lo que se lee bien (saltando las zonas que fallan para no insistir), después recorta los bordes de las zonas dañadas, luego las lee sector por sector y al final reintenta los sectores ilegibles. Así se rescata lo máximo con el mínimo castigo al disco. Los sectores que nunca se pudieron leer quedan en ceros y se anotan en *.malos.txt. El avance se guarda en *.mapa: si se interrumpe (o se corta la luz) se continúa exactamente desde ahí. Después agregás la imagen a la lista y recuperás desde ahí.
- Dejá de usar el disco dañado. Cada escritura nueva puede pisar lo que querés recuperar.
- Copiá siempre a otro disco. Reflota se niega a copiar al mismo disco que está leyendo.
- Si el disco hace ruidos raros o desaparece a cada rato, apagalo: ese es un problema físico y conviene un servicio profesional.
Hace
- Lee discos físicos, unidades USB, tarjetas e imágenes de disco (.img).
- Sigue adelante aunque haya sectores ilegibles: los rellena con ceros, marca el archivo como parcial y lo anota en recuperacion_log.csv.
- Si el sector de arranque está dañado, prueba la copia de respaldo (FAT32, exFAT) y otras ubicaciones típicas de la MFT (NTFS). FAT16/FAT12 no guardan copia del arranque.
- Muestra los archivos que no encuentran su carpeta en _huerfanos.
Sobre los archivos borrados
- Al borrar un archivo, el sistema suele conservar su nombre y dónde estaba el contenido, pero libera ese espacio. Si después se guardaron otros archivos encima, el contenido se pierde. Reflota lo detecta y lo muestra como recuperable, N% intacto o sobrescrito (los sobrescritos no se copian; los parciales sí, avisando).
- NTFS: usa los registros libres de la MFT y el mapa de espacio libre ($Bitmap). Es lo más confiable.
- FAT32, FAT16/12 y exFAT: usa las entradas de carpeta borradas. Estos formatos borran la cadena de clusters, así que Reflota asume que el archivo estaba en un solo bloque seguido; si estaba fragmentado, el resultado puede salir mezclado aunque diga "recuperable". En FAT32, un archivo con nombre corto (formato 8.3) pierde la primera letra del nombre al borrarse (queda _orrame.pdf).
- Si el disco se formateó o la carpeta que lo contenía ya no existe, los borrados pueden aparecer en _borrados (carpeta de origen desconocida).
- Siempre conviene recuperar a otro disco y dejar de usar el original apenas se nota el problema.
No hace (todavía)
- No recupera otros sistemas de archivos como ext4, APFS o ReFS, ni discos con BitLocker sin descifrar.
- La búsqueda por contenido no reconstruye nombres, carpetas ni fechas, y solo sabe unir pedazos de fotos JPEG baseline (no otros formatos fragmentados).
- No detecta formatos muy poco comunes en la búsqueda por contenido, ni los PSD con compresión ZIP ni los JPEG progresivos fragmentados.
- Los archivos cifrados (EFS) o comprimidos por NTFS se omiten y quedan en el log.
- No repara el disco ni arregla fallas físicas.
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --particiones
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --offset 608174080 --ls /Programacion --borrados
reflota.exe --source \\.\PhysicalDrive5 --offset 608174080 --copiar /Programacion --dest D:\Recuperado
Con Python 3.8+ (Windows):
python reflota.py              # correr directo, sin instalar nada
.\build_exe.ps1                # genera dist\Reflota.exe
El .exe se publica sin firma. Para firmarlo hace falta un certificado de firma de código (se compra, o se pide gratis para proyectos de código abierto a servicios como SignPath Foundation). Con el certificado en un .pfx se firma así (requiere signtool del Windows SDK):
.\firmar_exe.ps1 -Pfx C:\ruta\certificado.pfx
El script incluido está sin probar (no se pudo verificar sin un certificado real). Aun firmado, SmartScreen puede avisar un tiempo hasta que el programa gane reputación.
MIT: usalo, copialo y modificalo libremente. Ver LICENSE.
Reflota is a free, open-source, read-only file recovery tool for NTFS, FAT32, FAT16/FAT12 and exFAT. On NTFS it reads the whole $MFT and rebuilds the folder tree from each file's parent reference; on FAT32/exFAT it walks the directories and cluster chains. It also lists deleted files in their original folders and tells you how much of each is still intact. One tree shows disks → partitions → folders: tick a disk to copy everything, or tick only what you want; the size is computed automatically. It has a name search (wildcards, accent-insensitive, includes deleted files). It can also carve files by content (30+ formats including camera RAW, PSD and RAR, with exact lengths read from their structure, plus an optional, slower reassembly of fragmented baseline JPEGs), find lost partitions even with destroyed boot sectors, and make a safe, phased, resumable image (ddrescue-style: easy areas first, then trim, scrape, retry) of a failing disk. Recent additions were verified on synthetic test images, not yet on real hardware. Never writes to the source disk. Windows requires administrator rights for raw disk access; Reflota starts without them and asks only when you open a disk. MIT licensed.

articles.title: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
articles.body:
The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.
That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.
Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.
Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.
While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.
"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.
The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.
It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.
Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.
"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.
Used cars are not a steal
The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.
It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.
The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.
Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.
That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.
But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.
No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.
A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.
The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.
"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.
Why are new cars so expensive?
In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.
But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.
American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.
Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.
For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.
Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."
"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."
A challenging time for automakers
Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.
And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.
Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."
For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.
For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.
"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."
